---
title: "Optimal biomass-based climate change mitigation pathways are spatially heterogeneous due to localized technoeconomic and biophysical constraints"
date: last-modified
abstract: |
  The use of biomass for climate change mitigation offers substantial technical potential, but optimal deployment is highly dependent on spatial, technoeconomic, and biophysical constraints. Blanket climate policies frequently fail to capture this heterogeneity. Here we apply a spatially explicit techno-economic and consequential life cycle assessment framework deployed at a 0.1-degree resolution across the United States, Europe, India, and China. We evaluate the economic viability and carbon abatement potential of three distinct biomass utilization pathways: Bioenergy (BE), Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS), and Pyrogenic Carbon Capture and Storage with soil application of biochar (PyCCS). Localized constraints, such as distance to geological CO~2~ sinks, baseline grid carbon intensity, and native soil cation exchange capacity, dictate the economically optimal pathway. Traditional BE tends to dominate at low carbon prices, particularly in regions with high wholesale energy prices like Europe, or high grid carbon intensities like India. PyCCS emerges as a highly competitive transition technology at moderate carbon prices, and serves as the optimal long-term pathway in specific agro-ecological zones with degraded soils, such as southern China. Conversely, high capital costs and piecewise long-distance pipeline penalties act as severe barriers to BECCS, which only achieves universal dominance at high carbon prices (e.g., 150 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e) where carbon capture revenues finally overwhelm infrastructure penalties. Ultimately, effective climate mitigation requires localized policies that match biomass resources to their most efficient regional end-use.

```{r pipeline-setup}
#| include: false
# Model pipeline: each step below is a cached chunk that runs in its own R process (scripts/ run from the
# repository root) and reruns only when the files it depends on change. Fingerprints are content
# hashes for code and parameters (stable across git checkouts) and size + modification time for the
# large, untracked GIS layers. Logs go to results/logs/.
repo <- normalizePath("..")
test_runs <- 100 # iterations per region in a quick Monte Carlo run
mc_skip_file <- file.path(repo, "results", "logs", "mc_analysis.skip") # token in the MC chunk's cache key
fig_scenarios <- c("default") # scenarios for the main figures (see scripts/run_analyses.R)

files_in <- function(paths) {
  paths <- file.path(repo, paths)
  f <- unlist(lapply(paths, function(p) if (dir.exists(p)) list.files(p, recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE) else p))
  sort(f[file.exists(f)])
}
fp_hash <- function(...) unname(tools::md5sum(files_in(c(...)))) # content hash
fp_stat <- function(...) { # size + mtime, for large untracked data
  i <- file.info(files_in(c(...)))
  paste(basename(rownames(i)), i$size, as.numeric(i$mtime))
}
fp_model <- function() list(fp_hash("BiocharAG/R", "BiocharAG/inst/extdata", "BiocharAG/DESCRIPTION",
  "scripts/manuscript_figures.R"), fp_stat("GIS/processed"))

# vars: named list of settings assigned in the subprocess's global environment before code runs
# (the subprocess does not see this document's variables). List them in the chunk's cache.extra too.
run_step <- function(name, code, vars = list()) {
  if (name %in% "mc_analysis") {
    # Ask for the run size only when the chunk is stale: none (skip; downstream steps use the existing
    # results), quick (test_runs iterations, two regions) or full (hours). Without a display, set the
    # environment variable MC_RUN. A skip writes a new token to mc_skip_file, which is in the chunk's
    # cache key, so the next render asks again.
    choice <- Sys.getenv("MC_RUN")
    if (!nzchar(choice)) {
      if (!capabilities("tcltk") || !nzchar(Sys.getenv("DISPLAY"))) stop("No display for the Monte Carlo dialog: set MC_RUN to none, quick or full.")
      choice <- tcltk::tk_select.list(c("none", "quick", "full"), preselect = "none", title = "Monte Carlo run size")
    }
    if (!choice %in% c("none", "quick", "full")) stop("Monte Carlo run size not chosen; render cancelled.")
    message("Monte Carlo run size: ", choice)
    if (choice == "none") {
      dir.create(dirname(mc_skip_file), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
      writeLines(format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d%H%M%OS6"), mc_skip_file)
      return(invisible(NULL))
    }
    vars <- utils::modifyList(vars, list(test_mode = choice == "quick", test_runs = test_runs))
  }
  dir.create(file.path(repo, "results", "logs"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  log <- file.path(repo, "results", "logs", paste0(name, ".log"))
  callr::r(function(code, repo, vars) {
    setwd(repo); list2env(vars, envir = globalenv()); eval(parse(text = code), envir = globalenv())
  }, args = list(code = code, repo = repo, vars = vars), wd = repo, stdout = log, stderr = "2>&1")
  invisible(Sys.time())
}
```

# INTRODUCTION

Biochar has been widely promoted for climate change mitigation, with co-benefits for soil health and crop production when used as a soil amendment.[@woolf2010; @lehmann2021biochar] Globally, biochar has the sustainable technical potential for carbon sequestration and emissions reductions of up to 3.4–6.3 Pg CO~2~e. However, the costs, benefits and tradeoffs for biochar vary spatially, creating substantial heterogeneity in its feasibility at a given carbon price. This variability is further affected by the fact that biochar must compete with alternative uses for the limited supply of available waste biomass. Indeed, alternative uses of biomass, such as producing bioenergy with or without carbon capture and sequestration can also help to mitigate climate change and may provide greater climate mitigation, lower costs, and/or greater co-benefits in certain contexts.[@woolf2016] This depends on a number of different factors, including soil type, cropland productivity, climate, energy fuel mix, feedstock availability, distance to CO~2~ sinks for carbon capture and storage, energy prices and food prices. For example, bioenergy production may provide a greater climate benefit in regions that are highly dependent on carbon-intensive energy sources and have high soil fertility, whereas biochar is more favorable where low-fertility soils can benefit from its soil-health improvement.[@woolf2016]

It is, therefore, critical to understand where biochar could be the best use of resources from a climate mitigation perspective. Currently, most biochar assessments focus on the technical potential, without mapping out the tradeoffs or identifying optimal pathways based on location. While there are some biochar life-cycle assessments that account for alternative biomass uses, they are highly context-specific and difficult to scale up on[@peters2015; @lefebvre2021]. As such, this project aims to provide a detailed feasibility and tradeoff analysis across four regions (North America, India, China, and Europe) to map where biochar represents the most efficient use of biomass to reduce atmospheric greenhouse gasses (GHGs). These regions represent a diversity of geographic, socio-economic, and agro-ecological conditions for a broad assessment of how constraints, tradeoffs and benefits vary across regions. This work will allow policy-makers and practitioners to make scientifically-informed decisions about which mitigation pathways are best suited for their geographies. It can also help contextualize biochar's mitigation potential by identifying areas that maximize its climate benefits and realistically support its production and application.

# RESULTS

## Capital-intensive pathways are highly sensitive to discount rates and carbon prices

@fig-evap and @fig-si-evap-social illustrate the core vulnerability of CDR pathways to capital lock-out. Because both BECCS (heavy upfront infrastructure) and PyCCS (deferred agronomic value) are highly sensitive to the cost of capital, high discount rates act as a strong barrier to adoption, forcing a retreat to traditional bioenergy (BE) without high carbon prices. For example, in the USA, at a 2% social discount rate and a 30 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e carbon price, PyCCS covers a large extent of the US Midwest and South, with BECCS only being viable close to CO~2~ sinks. However, stepping up to the 8% market baseline eliminates PyCCS's advantage, replacing it with almost entirely with BE. The value of biochar relies heavily on liming and nutrient substitution benefits that are amortized over a 10-year agronomic impact duration. At an 8% or 15% discount rate, the present value of those future soil benefits is diminished, rendering the upfront thermal penalties of pyrolysis economically unviable at low carbon prices. At a 2% discount rate and intermediate carbon price (around 100 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e), BECCS is nearly universal across the US. At 15%, the BECCS dominance is fractured, with BE reclaiming the geographic margins (e.g., the Northeast and far West), and PyCCS remaining only in localized pockets where soil conditions make it particularly attractive. This occurs because, when capital is expensive, the penalty for long-distance pipelines becomes insurmountable until carbon prices reach the 150 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e range. By the time the carbon price reaches 150 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e, the maps become almost entirely red across all discount rates. At this pricing level, the high CDR capture efficiency overwhelms the high cost of capital, making BECCS the most economically attractive option.

## Biochar provides a mid-price transition technology option and a long-term solution for specific agro-ecological zones

@fig-evap (China) provides a counterpoint to the US results. It shows how soils with strong production constraints that can be alleviated by biochar can create a persistent competitive advantage for biochar, particularly when combined with large distances to CO~2~ storage sites. PyCCS performs a central role as a transition technology that peaks at intermediate carbon prices that are high enough to make its carbon sequestration competitive with BE, but not so high that the more efficient CDR of BECCS per unit biomass outcompetes it (@fig-macc). Nonetheless, while BECCS ultimately becomes the optimal technology across the entire US spatial domain at high carbon prices, PyCCS remains the most viable pathway in southern China across almost all price and discount rate scenarios. This demonstrates that PyCCS is not merely a transition technology, but the optimal long-term pathway for specific agro-ecological zones. In Southern China, characterized by highly weathered, acidic soils, the biochar's liming and nutrient use efficiency benefits provide a substantial economic credit that buffers against high processing costs. The model scales physical yield efficiency gains inversely to the soil's native Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC), thus granting severe CEC deficits higher premiums. This is confirmed by the SHAP analysis (@fig-shap-dominant), which identifies soil CEC as the dominant spatial driver in this region.

## Regional policies hinder biochar competitiveness

In India, on the other hand, the mid carbon price advantage of PyCCS is almost entirely eliminated, with BECCS eventually covering most of the map at high carbon prices. Here, fertilizer subsidies hamper PyCCS's economic viability. Because PyCCS economics relies on improved nutrient use efficiency and lower fertilizer inputs per unit crop yield, cheap subsidized synthetic fertilizers erode biochar's nutrient substitution value. Despite this, Biochar maintains a strong foothold in the regions in the North East, North West, and central Eastern coastal regions of India where low soil CEC is a major constraint to crop production.

## Regional energy prices and carbon intensity provide a critical constraint on the optimal CDR pathways

At lower carbon prices The optimal technology in Europe is almost universally BE, driven by high energy prices as the dominant driver across Europe. At 30 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e, the revenue from maximized power generation in BE outweighs the incentive to capture and sequester carbon, rendering the capital expenditure for BECCS and PyCCS unviable across all discount rates. As carbon prices increase, BECCS begins to dominate across central and northern Europe. PyCCS gains a strong advantage in Southern Europe, and Eastern Scandinavia where various combinations of large distances to CO~2~ sinks, already-low carbon intensity of the energy systems, and infertile soils make it more competitive. As in China, we see PyCCS maintain its advantage in these regions, even at very high carbon prices.

The value of bioenergy power also depends on how it is dispatched within the wider power system, which this plant-level analysis represents only approximately. Each plant here processes a fixed annual quantity of biomass, set by its capacity and capacity factor, and BE chooses between base-load and flexible operation on its own net value. In system models that optimise capacity and hourly dispatch together, biomass is a scarce, storable fuel that the system directs to the hours and uses where it is most valuable, such as periods of high residual load, so that its operating regime depends on the generation mix, demand and other sources of flexibility of each grid [@johansson2019; @lehtveer2021; @ahlstrom2022]. Where such flexibility is scarce, the value of BE, and of BECCS operated below base load, may therefore be higher than estimated here; where it is abundant, base-load operation, as assumed here, is closer to the system optimum.

## Plant size and CO~2~ infrastructure shift the technology mix

Three structural assumptions that the Monte Carlo analysis holds fixed were tested by repeating the carbon-price sweep (@fig-si-variants). Plant size has the largest effect. Larger plants favour the more capital-intensive technologies through economies of scale: with 250 MW~th~ instead of 125 MW~th~ plants, BECCS is adopted at lower carbon prices, and in the United States abatement at 150 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e rises from 46 to 337 Tg CO~2~e yr^-1^. With 50 MW~th~ plants, adoption is delayed and PyCCS keeps a larger share: in the United States at 200 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e, PyCCS provides 243 of 257 Tg CO~2~e yr^-1^, against 91 of 529 Tg CO~2~e yr^-1^ by default. In Europe, 250 MW~th~ BE plants are profitable even without a carbon price. Where almost all biomass is already used at high carbon prices, as in China and India above about 150 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e, plant size changes the timing of adoption but not the eventual abatement. These results should be read alongside the constraints on plant size that the model does not represent (see Methods): economies of scale favour ever larger plants, but road traffic, nuisance and local infrastructure limit the size of biomass plants in agricultural landscapes. Requiring each plant to build a dedicated pipeline to its sink, rather than share trunklines, delays BECCS and shifts biomass to PyCCS: at 150 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e, total abatement falls from 1,124 to 885 Tg CO~2~e yr^-1^ in China and from 287 to 209 Tg CO~2~e yr^-1^ in Europe. Allowing CO~2~-EOR as a sink raises abatement at intermediate carbon prices in China (from 731 to 821 Tg CO~2~e yr^-1^ at 100 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e) but by 5% or less in the other regions.

## Competing uses of crop residues

The analysis values crop residues against two counterfactuals: retention in the field, whose net soil GHG effect is close to zero [@mcclelland2025], and open burning, whose avoided CH~4~ and N~2~O emissions are credited. A third use, livestock fodder and bedding, is excluded from the supply: the sustainably harvestable residue of @karan2023, which is net of the fraction that must be retained to avoid soil degradation, is reduced by the fraction already used as fodder and bedding [@herrero2013]. This matters most in India, where cereal straws are a major source of fodder, whereas rice straw in the north-western rice–wheat belt is largely burned. Where the fodder fraction is underestimated locally, diverting residues would displace feed that must be replaced from other sources, with associated emissions, land use and costs; the net abatement estimated here is therefore most robust where residues would otherwise be burned or left in the field.

# DISCUSSION

The deployment of biomass for climate change mitigation cannot be guided by a single universal pathway. Our spatial analysis demonstrates that the economic viability of BE, BECCS, and PyCCS is dictated by a complex interplay of localized biophysical constraints and regional market dynamics.

While BECCS offers the highest theoretical carbon removal potential, its heavy infrastructure requirements and sensitivity to the cost of capital create significant barriers to entry, particularly where biomass is located far from suitable geological sinks. In contrast, PyCCS circumvents these transport constraints and establishes a resilient economic niche in regions with degraded, low-CEC soils, where its agronomic co-benefits—such as liming equivalence and nutrient substitution—offset its lower electrical conversion efficiencies. Southern China exemplifies this dynamic, demonstrating that PyCCS is a robust, long-term mitigation strategy for specific agro-ecological zones rather than merely a transition technology.

Furthermore, baseline energy markets shape optimal pathways. In Europe, high wholesale electricity prices establish BE as the dominant pathway at low carbon prices.

Biochar plants could also sell the heat from their surplus pyrolysis vapours and gases rather than generating electricity. In an exploratory scenario in which PyCCS sold all its heat to a year-round user, heat recovery raised the net value of PyCCS in all four regions, because heat earns more than electricity from the same fuel at a much lower capital cost, while abating slightly less, as heat displaces less CO~2~ per unit than electricity. Year-round heat demand, such as an industrial process or a district heating network, is uncommon in residue-producing regions, so heat recovery is an opportunity for co-location at particular sites rather than a basis for regional deployment, and it is not included in the results.

The soil N~2~O credit of PyCCS rests on short field trials. Most syntheses find that the reduction declines within a few years of a single application [@borchard2019; @kaur2023; @yang2025biochar], and we model this decline. Some studies, however, report that aged biochar increases N~2~O emissions [@song2016; @wang2024aging; @guo2023legacy], whereas the largest synthesis of long-term field experiments (4–12 years) finds reductions that diminish without reversing [@yang2025biochar]. A reversal would last for as long as the biochar remains in the soil, so even a small one would matter: in our model, a persistent 5% increase in emissions after the reduction has decayed would more than cancel the central estimate of the credit. Long-term trials of single applications are needed to resolve this.

Realizing the climate mitigation potential of global biomass requires moving beyond blanket technological mandates. Policymakers must adopt spatially explicit strategies that target BECCS deployment near geological sinks, incentivize PyCCS in agro-ecological zones suffering from soil degradation, and recognize the enduring role of BE in displacing highly carbon-intensive fossil grids.

# METHODS

## Objectives and design

The C-SCAPE model (Carbon Spatial Cost and Allocation Pathways Evaluator, version 1.0) compares three uses of crop residues: bioenergy (BE), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), and pyrolysis with soil application of the biochar. The last is a form of pyrogenic carbon capture and storage (PyCCS), a term that also covers other uses of pyrolysis products [@schmidt2019pyccs]. PyCCS is evaluated with and without energy export: pyrolysis vapors and gases supply the process heat, and the surplus is either exported as electricity or heat, or flared. For each grid cell and pathway, it calculates the net present value (NPV) per megagram of dry, ash-free feedstock, annualized with the capital recovery factor. Greenhouse gas emissions and removals are converted to 100-year CO~2~ equivalents and valued at a carbon price. Parameter values are listed in @tbl-parameters.

We applied the model to the coterminous United States, Europe, India and mainland China. Each region is restricted to its national territory, taken from the World Bank Official Boundaries [@worldbank2026boundaries]. Mainland China excludes Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau, for which we did not compile regional price data. Europe comprises the countries of geographic Europe within 11°W–40°E and 35–71°N, including Ukraine, Belarus and the part of Türkiye within these bounds, but not Russia.

All spatial inputs were resampled to a geographic (WGS84) grid of 0.1° (0.2° for the United States). Cell areas are calculated on the ellipsoid. Biomass collection distances were computed in equal-area projections (EPSG:5070 for the United States, EPSG:3035 for Europe, and Albers equal-area projections for China and India) and then transferred to the model grid. Maps omit islands smaller than 2,500 km^2^, which are too small to show at figure scale; all results include them. C-SCAPE is implemented as an R package in R 4.5 [@rcore2025], using the terra package for spatial analysis [@hijmans2025terra].

## Biomass feedstock sourcing and logistics

### Residue supply

Available crop residue is the sustainably harvestable residue of @karan2023, which excludes the fraction that must be retained to avoid soil degradation, minus the fraction fed to livestock. The livestock fraction of each world region is the stover feed use of @herrero2013 divided by the region's residue production. We apportion this regional fraction among residue types by palatability. Rice straw is poorly digestible and, where rice and wheat are grown together, is mostly burned rather than fed: in Punjab, 7% of rice straw is fed, against 45% of wheat straw [@kumar2015]. Rice straw therefore carries a weight of 0.2 relative to other residues, and rice husk, a milling residue, a weight of zero. The weighted fractions are scaled so that each region's livestock use is unchanged, and no residue type loses more than its harvestable fraction. In South Asia, where livestock use 28% of residue production, all harvestable wheat, maize and other cereal residue goes to livestock, so the residue available in India is almost entirely rice straw and husk. The modeled supply therefore does not divert residues from livestock feed; bedding is not represented separately.

### Biomass transport costs and emissions

Each plant draws its feedstock from a circular catchment that holds its annual feedstock demand,

$$M = \frac{3.6\, P\, h\, \phi}{L},$$ {#eq-feed-demand}

where $M$ is the annual feedstock demand (Mg yr^-1^, dry, ash-free), $P$ the thermal input capacity (MW~th~), $h$ = 8,760 h yr^-1^, $\phi$ the capacity factor, $L$ the lower heating value of the feedstock (GJ Mg^-1^), and 3.6 converts MWh to GJ. Available biomass was summed within circles of radius 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 150, 250 and 500 km around each cell, on a 10 km grid in each region's equal-area projection (see Objectives and design). The catchment radius $r$ at which the summed biomass equals $M$ was interpolated linearly in $r^2$, that is, in catchment area. Because $M$ depends on plant size and capacity factor only through their product, collection distances computed at a reference capacity factor of 0.70 for a series of plant sizes apply to any capacity factor: a plant of size $P$ operating at $\phi$ uses the distance for size $P\phi/0.70$, interpolated in the square root of plant size. For biomass spread evenly over a circle, the mean straight-line collection distance is $\bar{d} = 2r/3$. The road distance is $\tau \bar{d}$, where $\tau$ is the biomass-weighted mean ratio of road-path to straight-line distance from the truck routing described below: 1.18 in the United States, 1.23 in Europe, 1.50 in China and 1.32 in India, for 125 MW~th~ plants (within 3% for 50–250 MW~th~).

Haulage cost per megagram of feedstock is

$$C_{\mathrm{h}} = \lambda \left[ c_{\mathrm{f}} + c_{\mathrm{v}}\, \tau \bar{d} \left( s_{\mathrm{t}} k_{\mathrm{t}} + s_{\mathrm{f}} k_{\mathrm{d}} k_{\mathrm{g}} + s_{\mathrm{o}} k_{\mathrm{d}} \right) \right],$$ {#eq-haul}

where $\lambda$ is the regional haulage cost factor (@tbl-parameters), which scales both loading and trucking costs, $c_{\mathrm{f}}$ the loading and handling cost, $c_{\mathrm{v}}$ the variable trucking cost per kilometer of one-way distance, $s_{\mathrm{t}}$, $s_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $s_{\mathrm{o}}$ the shares of variable cost that are time-based, fuel and other distance-based costs, and $k_{\mathrm{t}}$, $k_{\mathrm{d}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{g}}$ terrain and road-access factors for travel time, road distance and climb. The loading and handling cost is 6.27 US\$ Mg^-1^ (4.59 US\$ Mg^-1^ of dry matter in 2012) [@beach2012]. The variable cost, 0.19 US\$ Mg^-1^ km^-1^ (0.12 US\$ Mg^-1^ km^-1^ for straw and stover in 2006), is the truck distance-variable cost of @searcy2007 and includes the empty return trip. Following @atri2024, time-based costs (driver wages and benefits, truck finance, insurance) are 64% of the variable cost, fuel 24%, and other distance-based costs (repairs, tires, tolls) 12%.

The factors $k_{\mathrm{t}}$, $k_{\mathrm{d}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{g}}$ represent terrain and road access, which a flat per-kilometer rate does not capture. For every candidate plant location and plant size, we routed travel from each field in the catchment to the plant as the least-time path on the global motorized friction surface of @weiss2020, at 30 arc-seconds. Weighted by biomass over the catchment, the routes give the travel time and road-path length per kilometre of straight-line distance, and the cumulative climb on the loaded and empty legs. Climb fuel is the energy to lift the loaded and empty truck over the cumulative ascent of each leg. Descents are not credited, because diesel trucks recover little energy on downhill grades. Each factor is normalized to a biomass-weighted mean of one within each region, where the level of road distance is set by $\tau$ and the level of cost by $\lambda$. The factors therefore redistribute haulage cost within a region, from flat, well-connected areas to rugged or poorly connected ones.

Haulage emissions, $E_{\mathrm{h}} = e\, \tau \bar{d}\, k_{\mathrm{d}} k_{\mathrm{g}}$, scale with fuel use, where $e$ is the emission factor of a heavy-duty diesel truck, 1.0 × 10^-4^ Mg CO~2~e Mg^-1^ km^-1^ [@glec2024]. They are deducted from the net abatement.

Biochar is assumed to return to the cropland that supplied the residue, as a backhaul in the feedstock trucks, which run year-round from field-edge storage. Its transport is therefore charged only the loading and handling cost. Its application to the fields is described under Biochar field application.

Each grid cell contributes only its own biomass to the regional totals, so a cell represents a share of a plant rather than a plant site, and the number of plants of each technology follows from the biomass allocated to that technology. The collection distance of each cell is calculated as if all the biomass in its catchment were available to the technology chosen for that cell. This is not so where some cells within the catchment are allocated to a different technology. A plant could then be built smaller, or keep its design size and draw on a larger catchment that overlaps those of plants of the other technology. Enlarging the catchment is the cheaper response, because haulage costs are small relative to the economies of scale in capital cost. If a fraction $f$ of the biomass in the catchment is available to the plant (allocated to its own technology or to none), the catchment area must increase by a factor of $1/f$, and the radius and collection distance by $1/\sqrt{f}$. This correction is not applied in the model, but we estimated its effect for 125 MW~th~ plants. Because the preferred technology is spatially coherent at the scale of a catchment, the biomass-weighted mean of $f$ over adopted cells is 0.89–1.00 across the carbon prices and discount rates of @fig-evap and @fig-si-evap-social. The resulting increase in mean collection distance, at most 11%, would raise haulage costs by at most 0.4 US\$ Mg^-1^. The approximation breaks down for small, isolated patches of one technology surrounded by another, where too little biomass is available to supply a plant of design size. Cells with $f < 0.5$, whose catchment radius would need to grow by more than 40%, hold 0–7% of the adopted biomass, split between PyCCS and BECCS; in practice, this biomass would be used by the surrounding technology.

### Fuel quality

Crop residues contain more ash than the wood chips usually burned in bioenergy plants, and their ash causes fouling and slagging in boilers [@baxter1998; @garcía2017; @luan2025a]. We represent this as a fuel-quality penalty on BE and BECCS, relative to a plant fired with wood chips. Base capital cost is increased by 10% for medium-ash feedstocks (2–10% ash, such as wheat straw and maize stover) and by 25% for high-ash feedstocks (above 10%, such as rice straw and husk). Electrical efficiency is reduced by 5% and 10% of its value, respectively [@dea2026]. Because capital cost is scaled on biomass input at a fixed reference efficiency (@eq-capex), the efficiency penalty reduces revenue but not capital cost; the same applies to the parasitic load of carbon capture (see Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS)). The medium-ash premium matches the 9% higher cost, per megawatt of fuel input, of straw-fired than wood-chip-fired combined heat and power plants in Danish technology data [@dea2020]. With the regional feedstock ash contents (see Spatial input data), the United States and Europe (5.3% and 5.8% ash) take the medium-ash penalty, and China and India (12.8% and 18.6%) the high-ash penalty. Operation and maintenance (O&M) costs carry no separate penalty: they are a fraction of capital cost, which already includes it, and straw-fired and wood-fired plants have the same ratio of O&M to investment cost [@dea2020].

### Feedstock prices and storage

Feedstock is priced at the field side (farm gate or road side); haulage to the plant is costed separately (see Biomass transport costs and emissions). For Europe, China and India, the prices are collection costs that exclude the margins of farmers and intermediaries. For the United States, where no comparable national cost estimate exists, the price is a farm-gate price that includes a grower premium, and is therefore somewhat higher than a cost-only estimate (@tbl-feedstock-price). The nutrients removed with the residue are charged separately in every region (see Residue minerals and ash return). Prices are quoted per megagram of dry matter and converted to the dry, ash-free basis of the model with the regional ash content (@tbl-parameters); haulage and storage costs are converted in the same way.

| Region | Basis | Original value | 2024 US\$ Mg^-1^ | Source |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|:---|
| United States | Farm-gate price of crop residues, excluding the payment for nutrients removed | US\$24 per dry short ton (2011) | 37 | @perlack2011 |
| Europe | Road-side cost of cereal straw, by country (three classes), excluding replacement fertilizer | €20, 37.5 and 62.5 Mg^-1^ dry matter (2012), less €12.1 | 13.9, 44.6 and 88.5 | @dees2017s2biom |
| China | Field-side cost of collecting corn straw, Nongan county, Jilin | ¥99.6 Mg^-1^ (2019) | 17.7 | @wang2022strawfeed |
| India | Field-side cost of baled paddy straw, Haryana | 34 US\$ Mg^-1^ (dry basis) | 34 | @sokhansanj2023 |

: Field-side feedstock prices. {#tbl-feedstock-price}

In the Billion-Ton Update, about 80% of the primary crop residue supply in the United States is profitable to collect at a farm-gate price of US\$45 per dry short ton, and 90% at US\$50 [@perlack2011]. The price is uniform across the country because the underlying POLYSYS model applies a single national price, raised until a large and reliable supply is offered. It comprises the harvest cost, a grower premium and a payment that compensates the grower for the nutrients removed with the residue, about US\$26 per dry short ton [@perlack2011]. We exclude the nutrient payment, because nutrient removal is charged explicitly and on the same basis in all four regions.

The S2Biom atlas maps road-side costs of cereal straw at NUTS-3 level by activity-based costing [@dees2017s2biom]. Its costs include fertilizer to replace the nutrients removed with the straw. Because nutrient removal is charged separately in every region, we subtract an estimate of this cost: €12.1 Mg^-1^ of dry matter, the N, P and K of the European straw (@tbl-parameters) at the World Bank's 2012 fertilizer prices [@worldbank2026pinksheet]. The Monte Carlo analysis samples it down to €7.9 Mg^-1^, the value of P and K alone, because the N included by S2Biom is not reported. We aggregated them to country level in three cost classes: the lowest for eastern Europe, Poland and the Baltic states; the middle class for most of central, northern and southern Europe, including France and Spain; and the highest for Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Countries without an S2Biom value are assigned by analogy: Kosovo to the lowest class, like Serbia and Croatia, and Cyprus to the middle class, like Greece. We assign Türkiye to the middle class, because the market price of loose straw sold as fodder, 1,500–1,750 TL Mg^-1^ in 2023 in Samsun province (about 65–76 US\$ Mg^-1^), rules out the lowest class [@tek2026saman].

The Chinese value is the field-side cost of raking, baling and loading corn straw from the StrawFeed supply-chain model, excluding ¥72.5 Mg^-1^ for transport to the plant [@wang2022strawfeed]. Like the European and Indian values, it excludes the margins of farmers and brokers: power plants in Northeast China pay about ¥300 Mg^-1^ delivered, and ¥200–300 Mg^-1^ at the plant gate in other major producing provinces [@wang2022strawfeed].

In India, the available residue is almost entirely paddy straw (see Residue supply). Paddy straw has little value as fodder in the north-western rice–wheat belt because of its high silica content, and is otherwise burned in the field. Its price is the field-side cost of baled straw estimated for bioenergy supply chains in Haryana [@sokhansanj2023]. The Monte Carlo range extends from about 12 US\$ Mg^-1^, the low value of paddy straw where it is burned [@erenstein2011], to about 50 US\$ Mg^-1^, the price of straw traded as fodder [@duncan2020; @lopes2023].

Year-round operation requires interim storage of residues harvested within a few weeks. Published storage costs range from about 3 to 42 US\$ Mg^-1^: 3–11 for farm-scale storage in the United States [@becerra2022; @brechbill2008; @beach2012], 18 for on-farm and 31 for purpose-built storage in the United Kingdom [@shackley2011], 34 for storage and handling [@kung2013], and about 42 for six months' storage of German straw, 36.4% of its total supply cost [@karras2024]. We add 15 US\$ Mg^-1^ for the United States and Europe. For China and India, this is scaled by the regional haulage cost factor (11 and 10 US\$ Mg^-1^), consistent with storage accounting for 20–30% of the delivered cost of paddy straw in India [@ceew2021exsitu].

## Technology pathways and thermodynamics

Each pathway converts a biomass input equivalent to 125 MW~th~, on a lower-heating-value basis for dry, ash-free feedstock (@tbl-parameters), into exported electricity and stored carbon in different proportions.

### Bioenergy (BE)

BE combusts the feedstock in a dedicated steam-cycle power plant and exports the electricity to the grid. The biomass carbon returns to the atmosphere as CO~2~. Net electrical efficiency is 30% [@dea2026], so each megagram of dry, ash-free feedstock generates $E = \eta L / 3.6$ MWh, where $\eta$ is the net efficiency and $L$ the lower heating value (18.6 GJ Mg^-1^ [@phyllis2]).

Capital cost scales with plant size from a reference plant of 50 MW~e~ net capacity fired with wood chips, the size and fuel of the reference biomass plant of @eia2026:

$$I = 50{,}000\, I_{\mathrm{ref}} \left( \frac{\eta_{\mathrm{ref}} P}{50} \right)^{0.7},$$ {#eq-capex}

where $I$ is the total capital cost (US\$), $I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference capital cost (US\$ kW~e~^-1^), $P$ is the biomass input (MW~th~), and $\eta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the net electrical efficiency (LHV). The reference capital cost is 4,700 US\$ kW~e~^-1^ in the United States, from @eia2026. In Europe it is 4,300 US\$ kW~e~^-1^: the cost of a Danish straw-fired plant of 132 MW~th~ [@dea2020], scaled to 50 MW~e~, with the straw premium removed using the Danish ratio of straw-fired to wood-fired plant costs. For China and India, where many more biomass plants have been built recently, it is the average installed cost of bioenergy plants commissioned in 2024: 2,200 and 1,900 US\$ kW~e~^-1^, respectively [@irena2025]. India's regulatory benchmark for rice-straw plants is lower still, about 925 US\$ kW~e~^-1^ [@cerc2024].

O&M costs, fixed and variable together, are assumed to be 4% of capital cost per year for all conversion technologies (BE, BECCS, and the pyrolysis unit and power block of PyCCS) and in every region (see Regional cost adjustment). This value lies within the range of reference biomass plants: about 3.5% for the EIA 50 MW plant at a capacity factor of 0.70 (fixed O&M of 141.5 US\$ kW^-1^ yr^-1^ plus 5.44 US\$ MWh^-1^) [@eia2023], 3.2–4.2% plus 3.8–4.7 US\$ MWh^-1^ for stoker and fluidized-bed boilers [@irena2012], and 4.4–4.6% for Danish 80 MW~th~ straw- and pellet-fired combined heat and power plants [@dea2020].

The capacity factor depends both on plant availability, which is 0.91 for biomass plants after planned and unplanned outages [@dea2026], and on how close to full output each technology operates on average. Historical capacity factors of biomass power plants, 0.50–0.64 in the United States and at Drax [@eia2026epm; @drax2025], reflect operation with low or no carbon prices. In decarbonizing grids, biomass power can operate either as a base-load generator at a high capacity factor [@daggash2019; @prado2023] or as a flexible generator that supplies hours of high residual load, reducing the need for expensive grid storage [@johansson2019; @lehtveer2021]. We therefore evaluate BE in both modes, and each grid cell takes the mode with the higher NPV. Base-load operation is assumed to have a capacity factor of 0.85, below the plant availability to allow for part-load operation. Flexible operation is assumed to have a capacity factor of 0.45, or about 3,900 full-load hours per year, as for biomass power that supplies high-price hours in a modeled 2050 European system [@lehtveer2021]. A plant that follows prices sells in high-price hours, so its realized price exceeds the time-averaged wholesale price. From hourly day-ahead prices in 24–31 European markets [@ember2026hourly], we estimated this price ratio as 1.05 for base load and 1.30 for flexible operation, and apply these ratios in all regions. Because abatement per unit feedstock is the same in both modes, the choice of mode does not depend on the carbon price. Supplementary Text S1 gives the derivation of these values and their Monte Carlo ranges.

### Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS)

BECCS adds post-combustion CO~2~ capture to the BE plant. Capture reduces net electrical efficiency, mainly to provide heat for solvent or sorbent regeneration and power to compress the CO~2~. We assume an efficiency penalty of 8 percentage points at a capture rate of 90% [@ieaghg2009], drawn from studies of current amine capture, consistent with costing BECCS as a mature technology. Reviews place the penalty for pulverized-coal plants at 7.7–11.9 percentage points, and the Boundary Dam 3 unit lost about 8 points with capture [@herzog2016]. Present technology loses about 10.8 points, falling to 7.2 with improved solvents, compression and heat integration [@tramosljika2021]. The Monte Carlo range extends from projected future penalties of 5.3–6.3 points [@li2024ccs] to the 12.8–15.9 points estimated with 2009 amine technology for dedicated biomass plants [@ieaghg2009].

The CO~2~ captured per megagram of feedstock is

$$M_{\mathrm{c}} = \tfrac{44}{12}\, f_{\mathrm{C}}\, \chi,$$ {#eq-capture}

where $f_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon mass fraction of the dry, ash-free feedstock [@phyllis2] and $\chi$ the capture rate. Capture, compression and flue-gas cleaning add a premium to the capital cost of a BE plant of the same biomass input (@tbl-parameters). The premium follows the IEAGHG evaluation of dedicated biomass power plants with post-combustion amine capture, in which capture raised total investment by 38–40% for a 75 MW~e~ bubbling fluidized-bed plant and a 250 MW~e~ circulating fluidized-bed plant [@ieaghg2009]. Because net output fell at the same time, specific capital cost per net kW~e~ rose by 114–126%, within the 45–130% range reported across biomass CCS technologies [@bhave2017]. Expressing the premium per unit of biomass input keeps it independent of the efficiency penalty. O&M costs are the same fraction of capital cost as for BE.

BECCS is assumed to operate at base load, at the design capacity factor of power plants with carbon capture [@petranova2020], because of its high capital cost and the need for steady operation of capture, pipeline and injection [@johansson2019; @prado2023] (Supplementary Text S1).

#### Carbon transport and geological storage

##### Storage sites and sink choice

Geological storage is represented by 45 storage basins across the four regions: onshore saline formations, onshore oil fields suitable for CO~2~-enhanced oil recovery (EOR), and offshore saline formations and depleted fields. Basin locations and storage types follow the OGCI CO~2~ Storage Resource Catalogue [@ogci2024csrc] and, for the United States, the USGS national assessment of geologic CO~2~ storage resources [@usgs2013co2]. Further basins, added for coverage, are located at operating or planned storage projects listed in the CO2RE facilities database of the Global CCS Institute [@gccsi2025co2re], such as Porthos, Northern Lights, Greensand, Ravenna CCS, HyNet and Bayou Bend. Petroleum basins with a substantial saline storage resource, such as the Ordos, Songliao, Tarim and Junggar basins in China, the Cambay Basin in India and the Permian Basin in the United States, serve as saline sinks as well as EOR sites.

Four combinations of transport and storage are evaluated for every grid cell: a pipeline to an onshore saline formation; a pipeline to an EOR site; a pipeline and ship to an offshore site; and a pipeline with a subsea section to an offshore site. For each cell and plant size, the plant uses the combination with the lowest combined cost of transport and storage for its CO~2~ flow. Results are reported both without and with EOR sites as sinks.

##### Pipeline routing

Pipeline routes were computed on a grid ten times finer than the model grid (0.02° for the United States, 0.01° elsewhere). We use two cost surfaces, one to choose each route and one to cost it, so that a route can avoid difficult terrain without the avoidance being charged as extra pipeline length. Slope from the 250 m Geomorpho90m dataset [@amatulli2020] is converted, for each 250 m pixel, into a construction-cost multiplier $F_{\mathrm{cost}}(\theta)$, which is piecewise linear in slope $\theta$: 1.0 at 0°, 1.05 at 5°, 1.2 at 10°, 1.6 at 17°, 2.3 at 25°, 3.2 at 35° and 4.0 at 45°. The pixel values are averaged to the routing grid, and additive premiums are applied above 2,500 m altitude. <!-- TODO (reference required): altitude construction-cost premiums. --> Averaged along the routes, the slope multipliers give construction-cost multipliers of 1.01–1.04 for the median route and at most 1.10–1.46 for 99% of routes in each region, consistent with the route-average factors of 1.3 for routes less than 20% mountainous and 1.5 for routes more than 50% mountainous in @ieaghg2002transmission. The routing surface adds a planning-risk premium for steep ground,

$$F_{\mathrm{route}} = F_{\mathrm{cost}} \left[ 1 + r_{\max}\, \sigma\!\left( \frac{\theta - 20^\circ}{3^\circ} \right) \right],$$ {#eq-route}

where $\sigma$ is the logistic function and $r_{\max} = 2$ the maximum premium; $F_{\mathrm{route}}$ is capped at 25.

Protected areas from the World Database on Protected Areas [@wdpa2026] are tiered. Strictly protected areas (IUCN categories Ia, Ib and II, and natural World Heritage sites) are barriers. Other designated terrestrial protected areas can be crossed at a construction-cost premium of 25% and a routing premium of 100%. Marine protected areas do not affect the land routing.

Least-cost paths on $F_{\mathrm{route}}$ from every cell to the nearest target were computed with terra [@hijmans2025terra]. Tracing the resulting route tree gives, for each route, its physical length $L$, the line integral of $F_{\mathrm{cost}}$ along it, and the highest point of the route above the source, which sets the booster pumping requirement (see Pipeline network architecture). Pipeline cost is charged on $L$ multiplied by the route-average construction-cost multiplier, the line integral of $F_{\mathrm{cost}}$ divided by $L$; no further tortuosity factor is applied. Setting $r_{\max}$ to any value between 0 and 2 changed the optimal technology in less than 0.4% of grid cells.

##### Pipeline network architecture

Cost functions that scale pipeline cost linearly with length represent regional networks well but underestimate the cost of long-distance transport, which needs intermediate booster compression to overcome the frictional pressure drop. We therefore represent pipeline transport as a network of dedicated feeder pipelines and shared trunklines. Each plant builds a dedicated feeder pipeline over the first 50 km, whose capital cost scales with the plant's own CO~2~ flow; a plant within 50 km of its sink builds a dedicated pipeline throughout. Beyond 50 km, the plant joins a trunkline sized for 3 Tg CO~2~ yr^-1^ and pays a share of its capital cost proportional to its flow. Beyond 700 km, the marginal trunkline cost is doubled to represent booster stations. For routes longer than the feeder, the capital cost of pipeline transport attributable to a plant is

$$I_{\mathrm{p}} = \bar{F}_{\mathrm{cost}}\, c_0 \left[ d_{\mathrm{f}} \left( \frac{q}{q_0} \right)^{0.6} + \frac{q}{Q} \left( \frac{Q}{q_0} \right)^{0.6} \left( \min(L, 700) - d_{\mathrm{f}} + 2 \max(L - 700, 0) \right) \right],$$ {#eq-trunk}

where $\bar{F}_{\mathrm{cost}}$ is the route-average construction-cost multiplier (see Pipeline routing), $c_0$ the capital cost per kilometer of a pipeline carrying $q_0$ = 1 Tg CO~2~ yr^-1^, $d_{\mathrm{f}}$ = 50 km the feeder length, $q$ the plant's CO~2~ flow, $Q = \max(q, 3)$ Tg CO~2~ yr^-1^ the trunkline flow, and $L$ the route length (km). For routes of 50 km or less, $I_{\mathrm{p}} = \bar{F}_{\mathrm{cost}}\, c_0\, L\, (q/q_0)^{0.6}$. The reference cost $c_0$ is US\$50 million per 100 km, scaled by the regional capital cost factor (see Regional cost adjustment). It lies within the range of the diameter-based cost function of @solomon2024 (2.16 € m^-1^ per mm of diameter, in 2024 euros) for the 200–250 mm pipeline needed to carry 1 Tg yr^-1^ of dense-phase CO~2~ at typical velocities: 0.43–0.54 million € (0.47–0.58 million US\$) per km. Pipeline O&M costs are 4% of capital cost per year, as for the plants, and pipeline capital cost is annualized over the plant lifetime. <!-- TODO (reference required): scaling exponent, trunk scale, booster threshold and penalty, O&M fraction. -->

Routes that climb require booster pumping to restore the pressure lost in lifting dense-phase CO~2~. Pumps are sized for the lift beyond a 1 MPa design margin, with pump capital cost following @mccollum2006, and their electricity is charged at the regional electricity price.

##### Maritime shipping and subsea pipelines

CO~2~ bound for an offshore sink is either shipped or carried by a pipeline with a subsea section. The transport costs per megagram of CO~2~ are

$$C_{\mathrm{ship}} = C_{\mathrm{p}}(L_{\mathrm{port}}) + c_{\mathrm{liq}} + c_{\mathrm{term}} + c_{\mathrm{voy}}\, d_{\mathrm{sea}}, \qquad C_{\mathrm{sub}} = C_{\mathrm{p}}(L_{\mathrm{land}} + d_{\mathrm{sea}}),$$ {#eq-offshore}

where $C_{\mathrm{p}}(L)$ is the pipeline transport cost per megagram over a route of length $L$ (from @eq-trunk), $L_{\mathrm{port}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{land}}$ are the physical lengths of the onshore routes to the port or landfall, $d_{\mathrm{sea}}$ is the sea distance from there to the sink, $c_{\mathrm{liq}}$ is the liquefaction cost, $c_{\mathrm{term}}$ the fixed cost of ships, buffer storage and terminals, and $c_{\mathrm{voy}}$ the voyage cost per kilometer (@tbl-parameters). Sea distances were routed on a 0.02–0.04° grid with land impassable. The liquefaction cost is assumed to be 21 US\$ Mg^-1^ (2021) [@chen2021liquefaction]. The fixed and voyage costs are the intercept and slope of the ship transport cost, excluding liquefaction, of a 2.5 Tg yr^-1^ point-to-point chain: 8.2 € Mg^-1^ at 180 km, rising to 14.5 € Mg^-1^ at 1,500 km (2009 euros) [@zep2011transport]. Liquefaction and fixed costs are scaled by the regional capital cost factor. In $C_{\mathrm{sub}}$, each subsea kilometer carries 1.5 times the onshore capital cost per kilometer, within the range of 1.4–1.7 for offshore relative to onshore pipelines [@vito2026emis].

Every coastal cell is a candidate port or landfall. The land route and the port are chosen together, by a least-cost search from all coastal cells in which each coastal cell starts with its sea leg already priced, in equivalent kilometers of flat onshore pipeline: 0.2 km per sea kilometer for shipping (the ratio of the voyage cost to the trunk-pipeline cost per megagram-kilometer) and 1.5 km for subsea pipelines. The route therefore minimizes the combined cost of the land and sea legs rather than the land distance alone. The fixed liquefaction and terminal costs do not affect this choice.

Emissions from CO~2~ transport are deducted from the BECCS abatement. For shipping, the emissions from liquefaction, loading and the voyage are a fixed fraction of the CO~2~ carried plus a fraction per kilometer of voyage (@tbl-parameters): about 2.5% of the CO~2~ carried over 200 km and about 18% over 12,000 km [@albaroudi2021]. For pipelines, they are the emissions from the booster pumping electricity, at the displaced grid intensity.

##### CO~2~ storage costs

CO~2~ storage is costed per megagram of CO~2~ injected, separately from capture and transport. The cost covers injection wells and operations, and measurement, monitoring and verification, and it is applied to the mass of CO~2~ captured. The main driver of storage cost is whether a reservoir has open boundaries, which let the pressure raised by injection dissipate into the surrounding aquifer, or closed boundaries [@gccsi2025]. In a lifecycle assessment from exploration to 50 years of post-closure monitoring, storage costs 2–15 US\$ Mg^-1^ onshore and 5–31 US\$ Mg^-1^ offshore (2024 USD) in open reservoirs. It rises to 5–33 and 8–50 US\$ Mg^-1^, respectively, in closed reservoirs of moderate quality, and to as much as 58 and 147 US\$ Mg^-1^ in the least favorable closed reservoirs [@gccsi2025]. Earlier estimates for European saline aquifers, 2–12 € Mg^-1^ onshore and 6–20 € Mg^-1^ offshore, are consistent with these ranges [@zep2011]. Sinks without site-specific evidence take a default onshore or offshore cost within these ranges (@tbl-parameters).

We assign a site-specific cost to a sink where the evidence allows. For onshore saline formations in the United States, the cost is the first-year break-even price of the cheapest formation in the sink's state with at least 1 Pg of prospective storage resource, or in the basin where no formation in the state qualifies. These prices come from a formation-by-formation model that accounts for pressure build-up and interference [@netl2024scom], escalated from 2023 to 2024 USD. They range from 6.4 US\$ Mg^-1^ for the Frio Formation (Gulf Coast Basin) to 30.6 US\$ Mg^-1^ for the Simpson Sandstone (Anadarko Basin). Elsewhere, saline formations are classed as open where they are regionally extensive and well connected: the Utsira and Johansen formations of the northern North Sea, the Dogger aquifer of the Paris Basin and the Miocene sands of the Gulf of Mexico shelf. They are classed as closed where they are compartmentalized or of low permeability: the Buntsandstein of the North German Basin and the Liujiagou sandstone of the Ordos Basin. Each class takes the midpoint of its range above, 8.5 US\$ Mg^-1^ onshore and 18 US\$ Mg^-1^ offshore for open formations and 19 US\$ Mg^-1^ onshore for closed formations. Depleted oil and gas fields are not closed reservoirs in this sense, because they start below their original pressure. The six depleted fields among the sinks take 16.2 US\$ Mg^-1^, the mean of ZEP's offshore cases with and without reusable wells (€6 and €10 Mg^-1^ in 2009) [@zep2011], converted to 2024 USD. All other sinks, including every sink in India and all but one in China, take the default costs. CO~2~ delivered for EOR is charged the default onshore cost.

Each grid cell is charged the storage cost of the sink that its chosen transport and storage combination reaches (see Storage sites and sink choice). Because storage costs differ between sinks, the route search starts each sink at its storage cost, expressed as an equivalent length of flat onshore trunk pipeline at 0.05 US\$ Mg^-1^ km^-1^ (160 km for 8 US\$ Mg^-1^). A farther sink with cheaper storage can therefore be chosen. In the Monte Carlo analysis, the site-specific costs are scaled by a common sampled factor, and the default costs are sampled directly (@tbl-parameters).

### Pyrogenic carbon capture and storage (PyCCS)

PyCCS pyrolyzes the feedstock: heating it in the absence of oxygen converts it to biochar, condensable vapors (bio-oil) and permanent gases. Product yields follow the pyrolysis model of @woolf2014, which closes the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen balances. Biochar yield is an empirical function of the peak pyrolysis temperature, $T_{\mathrm{py}}$, and the lignin fraction of the feedstock. The carbon and hydrogen contents of the biochar are functions of $T_{\mathrm{py}}$ alone, with oxygen by difference, and the yields of hydrogen, carbon monoxide, methane and ethylene are also empirical functions of $T_{\mathrm{py}}$ [@woolf2014]. The carbon, hydrogen and oxygen not accounted for by the biochar and these gases are partitioned among bio-oil, CO~2~ and water. Bio-oil is assumed to have 1.25 times the carbon and 1.26 times the hydrogen mass fraction of the feedstock [@woolf2014]. This fixes its composition, so the three element balances can be solved for the yields of bio-oil, CO~2~ and water. We assume a peak pyrolysis temperature of 500 °C, representing the medium-temperature class (450–600 °C) of @woolf2021greenhouse and the IPCC inventory guidance [@ipcc2019biochar]. Yields and energy flows are expressed per megagram of dry, ash-free feedstock, and the feedstock ash reports to the biochar.

The energy balance is on a higher heating value (HHV) basis. The process heat demand is the HHV of the products (biochar, bio-oil and permanent gases) plus the process heat losses, minus the HHV of the feedstock. The HHVs of biochar and bio-oil are calculated from their carbon, hydrogen and oxygen fractions with the correlation of @channiwala2002, and that of the gas from the heats of combustion of its components. The feedstock HHV is its lower heating value (LHV) plus the latent heat of the water formed from its hydrogen. Heat losses comprise three terms. The first is conduction through the insulated reactor wall, whose area is sized from the plant feed rate and a temperature-dependent solids residence time. The second is the sensible heat of biochar discharged at $T_{\mathrm{py}}$. The third is the heat carried by the bio-oil vapor, permanent gases and water vapor (feedstock moisture plus reaction water) leaving the heat-recovery system, including the latent heat of the vapors. Because this term includes the latent heat of all water leaving the process, expressing both feedstock and products on an HHV basis avoids counting that latent heat twice. Process heat is supplied by combusting the pyrolysis vapors and gases in a process heater, and the plant's parasitic electricity demand is met from the same fuel [@woolf2014]. If the vapors and gases cannot meet these loads, part of the biochar is combusted, which reduces the biochar yield in proportion.

The surplus vapors and gases, converted to an LHV basis, are combusted in a power block that raises steam for a condensing turbine. A power block is not always worthwhile: where electricity prices are low or the displaced grid intensity is small, its capital cost can exceed its revenue and grid credit. PyCCS is evaluated in each grid cell both with the power block and without energy export, in which case the surplus is flared. Export of heat alone is not included in the main results, because a heat-recovery boiler and a heat distribution network are justified only where there is a reliable year-round demand for heat. Such demand is a special case rather than a general condition (an exploratory heat-export scenario is reported in the Discussion). The configuration with the higher net value at the given carbon price is used. Because electricity is a small share of PyCCS revenue, operation is limited by the availability of the pyrolysis unit and the continuity of biomass supply rather than by dispatch. PyCCS is therefore assumed to operate at a capacity factor of 0.80, below the 0.90 on-stream factor of nth-plant pyrolysis designs [@dutta2015], to allow for interruptions of feedstock supply (Supplementary Text S1).

The pyrolysis unit costs 335 US\$ per Mg yr^-1^ of feed capacity in the United States (2024 USD), at the feed rate of a 50 MW~e~ reference plant. This is NREL's nth-plant estimate for a 2,000 Mg day^-1^ (dry basis) slow pyrolysis plant [@yadav2026], scaled to the reference size with an exponent of 0.7. The power block costs 3,250 US\$ kW~e~^-1^ in the United States. This lies between the cost of a steam cycle alone in NREL's pyrolysis designs, about 2,650 US\$ kW~e~^-1^ [@dutta2015], and that of a complete 50 MW~e~ biomass power plant [@eia2026], which also includes solid-fuel handling (4,700 US\$ kW~e~^-1^). The power block cost scales with size according to @eq-capex, with $P$ the fuel input to the power block and $\eta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ its own net electrical efficiency (@tbl-parameters). Both costs are scaled to other regions by the capital cost location factor (see Regional cost adjustment).

#### Biochar carbon storage

We consider only soil application of biochar, because its agronomic value is part of the comparison between pathways. Biochar carbon in soil decays slowly, and we credit the fraction remaining after 100 years, $F_{\mathrm{perm}}$, following the method of @woolf2021greenhouse. That method uses incubation experiments in which the loss of biochar carbon was fitted with multi-pool exponential decay models. The decay rates of each experiment are adjusted from the incubation temperature to the mean annual soil temperature of the grid cell with a temperature-dependent $Q_{10}$. The fraction remaining after 100 years is then calculated for each experiment and regressed linearly on the molar ratio of hydrogen to organic carbon (H:C~org~) of the biochar. 

The CO~2~ stored per megagram of feedstock is

$$S_{\mathrm{bc}} = \tfrac{44}{12}\, C_{\mathrm{bc}}\, F_{\mathrm{perm}},$$

where $S_{\mathrm{bc}}$ is in Mg CO~2~ Mg^-1^, $C_{\mathrm{bc}}$ is the biochar carbon yield (Mg C Mg^-1^), net of any biochar combusted to close the energy balance, and 44/12 converts carbon to CO~2~.

#### Biochar field application

The biochar produced from the residue of a grid cell is applied to the cropland of that cell. Its amount per hectare of cropland is

$$b = \kappa\, q_{\mathrm{h}}\, Y_{\mathrm{bc}},$$ {#eq-bc-supply}

where $b$ is the biochar available per hectare of cropland (Mg ha^-1^ yr^-1^), $\kappa$ the cropping intensity (harvests per year), $q_{\mathrm{h}}$ the available residue per hectare of harvested area (Mg ha^-1^ yr^-1^, dry, ash-free; see Residue supply) and $Y_{\mathrm{bc}}$ the biochar yield (Mg Mg^-1^ of feedstock). Residue supply is expressed per hectare of harvested area, the basis of the crop-specific residue data [@karan2023]. The cropping intensity converts it to physical cropland, on which biochar accumulates. Where the residue and harvested-area maps disagree, $q_{\mathrm{h}}$ is capped at a physically plausible maximum (@tbl-parameters). The feedstock supplied per hectare of cropland is $m = b / Y_{\mathrm{bc}}$ (Mg ha^-1^ yr^-1^).

The biochar is applied to the cropland in rotating cohorts. For a dose $D$ per application (Mg ha^-1^), the cropland is divided into $\nu = \lceil D/b \rceil$ cohorts of equal area. Each cohort receives $D_{\mathrm{e}} = \nu\, b$ every $\nu$ years during the plant lifetime, $t_{\mathrm{L}}$. A dose at or below $b$ corresponds to annual application to all cropland. Larger doses need fewer field operations per megagram of biochar, but deliver less yield benefit per megagram, because the yield response is concave in dose (see Biochar agronomic valuation). We evaluated five application strategies: annual application to all cropland, and rotating application at 2.5, 5, 10 and 20 Mg ha^-1^. At each carbon price, the strategy with the highest net value is used. Doses are expressed as mass of biochar, the basis of the field trials from which the yield and N~2~O responses were derived.

Biochar is assumed to remain where it is applied, and successive applications to the same land are assumed to act as one application of their cumulative amount. The effective biochar stock of cohort $j$ in year $t$ is

$$B_{j,t} = \sum_{i:\, t_i \le \min(t,\, t_{\mathrm{L}})} D_{\mathrm{e}}\, e^{-(k + k_{\mathrm{y}}/\gamma)(t - t_i)},$$ {#eq-bc-stock}

where $B_{j,t}$ is in Mg ha^-1^, $t_i$ are the application years of the cohort, $k = -\ln F_{\mathrm{perm}}/100$ is the mean decay rate of biochar carbon implied by the 100-year permanence factor (see Biochar carbon storage), $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ is the rate at which the yield response declines beyond the loss of biochar carbon (yr^-1^; see Biochar agronomic valuation), and $\gamma$ is the dose exponent of @eq-dose-shape. Because the response increases with the stock as a power function with exponent $\gamma$, a stock decaying at $k_{\mathrm{y}}/\gamma$ gives a response that declines at $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ after a single application. The stock outlasts the plant, so its effects are evaluated over a horizon $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ of 100 years.

Each application is a spreading pass, assumed to be timed to precede tillage, which incorporates the biochar into the soil. Most cropland is tilled at least every few years. Four-fifths of the US area of corn, soybeans, cotton and wheat was tilled at least once in four years during 2012–2017 [@claassen2018], and conventional or conservation tillage is used on most arable land in the European Union [@eurostat2020tillage]. Fields classed as no-till are also tilled occasionally, for example to control herbicide-resistant weeds [@dang2018]. Because each cohort is treated only every $\nu$ years, its application can wait for a cultivation year, so we do not charge for incorporation. Prompt incorporation also limits losses of surface biochar by wind and runoff [@major2010]. The cost per hectare and pass, $c_{\mathrm{s}}$, is the spreading share, 70%, of the cost of spreading and incorporating biochar [@woolf2016optimal], scaled to each region by the haulage cost factor (see Regional cost adjustment); the share is that of spreading in the diesel use of spreading and incorporation [@leppakoski2021]. Each hectare receives $1/\nu$ passes per year. The tractor diesel per pass is the same share of 17.5 L ha^-1^, the median of published estimates for spreading and incorporation [@roberts2010; @pujolpereira2016; @leppakoski2021; @cheng2025], and its emissions are deducted from the net abatement.

#### Soil N~2~O emissions

Biochar additions reduce direct emissions of nitrous oxide (N~2~O) from fertilized soils. We estimated the reduction from field trials by multilevel random-effects meta-analysis of the data compiled by @xu2021 (Supplementary Text S3). The mean reduction, $R_{\mathrm{N_2O}}$, is 20% (90% confidence interval 11–29%; 36 studies). It did not vary detectably with dose between 2.2 and 72 Mg ha^-1^. Any application at or above the lowest dose tested, $D_{\mathrm{N}}$ = 2.2 Mg ha^-1^, is therefore assumed to give the full reduction, and smaller doses a reduction proportional to dose.

Too few trials in these data extend beyond one year to show whether the reduction declines as biochar ages (6 studies). Other syntheses find that it does, although they differ on how quickly: the reduction has been reported to become negligible within about a year [@borchard2019; @liu2020n2o], or to peak about 1.5 years after application and decline thereafter [@kaur2023], and it diminishes over time after single applications [@yang2025biochar]. At some sites, however, reductions persist 7–8 years after a single application [@guo2023legacy; @zhang2026paddy]. We assume that the reduction declines exponentially after each application, with a half-life $t_{1/2}$ of 2 years (1–10 years in the Monte Carlo analysis; @tbl-si-mc), and that the next application to the same land restores it. The avoided emissions per megagram of feedstock are

$$A_{\mathrm{N_2O}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{app}}\, \mathit{EF}_1\, R_{\mathrm{N_2O}}\, \min\!\left(1, D_{\mathrm{e}}/D_{\mathrm{N}}\right)}{m\, t_{\mathrm{L}}} \sum_{t=1}^{t_{\mathrm{H}}} \bar{\phi}_t \cdot \frac{44}{28} \cdot \mathrm{GWP}_{\mathrm{N_2O}} \cdot 10^{-3},$$ {#eq-n2o}

where $A_{\mathrm{N_2O}}$ is in Mg CO~2~e Mg^-1^, $N_{\mathrm{app}}$ is the regional mineral N application rate per hectare of cropland (kg N ha^-1^ yr^-1^), $\mathit{EF}_1$ the IPCC Tier 1 direct emission factor (kg N~2~O-N kg^-1^ N) [@ipcc2019], and $\bar{\phi}_t$ the mean over cohorts of $e^{-\lambda (t - t_j)}$, with $t_j$ the latest application year of cohort $j$ up to year $t$ and $\lambda = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$. Cohorts not yet treated contribute zero. The factor 44/28 converts N~2~O-N to N~2~O, $\mathrm{GWP}_{\mathrm{N_2O}}$ is the 100-year global warming potential of N~2~O [@forster2021], and 10^-3^ converts kilograms to megagrams. Avoided emissions are summed without discounting, as for biochar carbon storage, and attributed to the feedstock processed over the plant lifetime.

#### Biochar agronomic valuation

The agronomic value of biochar per megagram of feedstock is

$$V_{\mathrm{ag}} = V_{\mathrm{lime}} + V_{\mathrm{nut}} + V_{\mathrm{CEC}} - V_{\mathrm{s}},$$ {#eq-vag}

where $V_{\mathrm{lime}}$ is the liming value, $V_{\mathrm{nut}}$ the nutrient value, $V_{\mathrm{CEC}}$ the value of the crop yield increase from raising the cation exchange capacity (CEC) of the soil, and $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ the cost of field application (all US\$ Mg^-1^ of feedstock). Agricultural lime and mineral fertilizer substitute for biochar as a pH amendment and as a nutrient source, so $V_{\mathrm{lime}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{nut}}$ are the costs of the inputs that biochar displaces. Biochar also raises the CEC of soils, improving their retention and supply of nutrients and water. Fertilizer is not a substitute for CEC but a complementary input: a soil with low CEC retains and supplies nutrients poorly and responds poorly to fertilizer, so raising its CEC lifts the whole fertilizer response curve, including the economically optimal application rate. $V_{\mathrm{CEC}}$ is therefore valued as a yield increase rather than as a displaced input. The nutrients and alkalinity removed with the residue are charged to all pathways (see Residue minerals and ash return).

Where soil pH is below the target pH (@tbl-parameters), the acid-neutralizing capacity of the biochar (@eq-anc) is credited at the cost of agricultural lime; elsewhere the liming value is zero. The full capacity is credited, without a cap at the lime requirement of the soil, because fertilizer N keeps acidifying the soil: each kilogram of N dissolves about 1.8 kg of CaCO~3~ [@zamanian2018], or 0.11–0.35 Mg ha^-1^ yr^-1^ at the regional N application rates. At the median biochar supply, the alkalinity returned to each hectare of cropland, 0.03–0.11 Mg CaCO~3~-eq yr^-1^, is 15–40% of this acidification, and bottom ash returns similar amounts, so the returned alkalinity substitutes for maintenance liming that would otherwise be needed. Across the four regions, this capacity is 17–36 kg CaCO~3~-eq Mg^-1^ of feedstock, a calcium carbonate equivalent of 5–8% of the biochar. Because substituting biochar for lime also avoids hauling and spreading the lime, the lime cost includes transport and application. It is the median of published values (@tbl-parameters), each converted to a calcium carbonate equivalent of 100% and escalated to 2024 USD. These values range from 31 US\$ Mg^-1^ for lime delivered to Brazilian pastures, excluding spreading [@latawiec2019], through 52 US\$ Mg^-1^ in Oklahoma [@mills2020lime] and 59–110 US\$ Mg^-1^ near to and far from a quarry in Oklahoma [@cho2020lime], to 85 US\$ Mg^-1^ spread in North Carolina [@woods2026]. The Monte Carlo analysis samples this range.

The biochar retains all of the P and K of the feedstock (see Residue minerals and ash return). P and K are credited at their total content. Whether they are returned in biochar, in ash or in retained residue, they remain in the soil and become available to crops over the following years; the nutrients removed with the residue are valued on the same basis. Biochar N is held mainly in heterocyclic aromatic structures and is assumed to have no fertilizer value. P and K are valued at the world market prices of triple superphosphate and potassium chloride, respectively, averaged over the World Bank's annual prices for 2021–2025 and escalated to 2024 USD [@worldbank2026pinksheet]. Elemental P and K are converted to their oxide equivalents (×2.29 for P~2~O~5~ and ×1.20 for K~2~O) before pricing. We use the same prices in every region. Retail subsidies (as in India) and export controls (as in China) move farm-gate prices away from world prices, but they transfer value rather than change the economic value of the fertilizer displaced.

The yield response to biochar was derived from a meta-analysis of field trials that combines the data of @woolf2016optimal, @xu2021 and @zhang2023 (Supplementary Text S3). The response increases with the biochar stock as a power function and decreases in magnitude with soil CEC. The relative yield increase of cohort $j$ in year $t$ is

$$\frac{\Delta y_{j,t}}{y} = e^{\alpha\, g(B_{j,t})} - 1, \qquad \alpha = \max\!\left(0,\ \beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{C}} \ln \mathrm{CEC}\right),$$ {#eq-yield-response}

$$g(B) = \begin{cases} (B/B_{\mathrm{r}})^{\gamma}, & B \ge B_{\mathrm{min}} \\ (B_{\mathrm{min}}/B_{\mathrm{r}})^{\gamma}\, B / B_{\mathrm{min}}, & B < B_{\mathrm{min}}, \end{cases}$$ {#eq-dose-shape}

where $\Delta y_{j,t}/y$ is the fractional increase in crop yield, $\alpha$ the natural logarithm of the ratio of yields with and without biochar at the reference stock $B_{\mathrm{r}}$ = 10 Mg ha^-1^, CEC the soil CEC (cmol~c~ kg^-1^), $\beta_0$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{C}}$ fitted coefficients, $\gamma$ the dose exponent, and $B_{\mathrm{min}}$ the smallest stock to which the power function is applied (@tbl-parameters). Below $B_{\mathrm{min}}$, $g$ increases linearly from zero. Few trials tested doses this small, and extending the power function to them would imply an unbounded yield benefit per megagram as the dose approaches zero. The exponent $\gamma$ is that fitted to trials on soils with a pH of 6.5 or above, where liming does not contribute to the response. The acid-soil component of the response is excluded from $\alpha$, because it is credited as the liming value. The response falls to zero at a CEC of about 36 cmol~c~ kg^-1^.

The yield increase is valued at $v_{\mathrm{c}}$, the value of crop production per hectare of harvested area, at production-weighted international prices of the major field crops (see Spatial input data). We do not assume that biochar goes to high-value horticultural crops. They occupy too little land to absorb biochar at the scale modeled here and are rarely grown on the resource-poor soils where the response is largest. The yield value per megagram of feedstock follows from @eq-ag-level, with the annual benefit per hectare of cropland $x_t = \kappa\, v_{\mathrm{c}}$ multiplied by the mean of $\Delta y_{j,t}/y$ over cohorts. The cost of field application, $V_{\mathrm{s}}$, follows from the same equation with $x_t = c_{\mathrm{s}}/\nu$ during the plant lifetime and zero after it.

The CEC of biochar increases rather than declines as it ages in soil, as oxidation adds functional groups to its surfaces [@cheng2006; @liang2006], so the CEC component of the yield response is expected to persist. Its effect on crops can nonetheless decline, because aggregates and mineral coatings occlude biochar surfaces [@brodowski2006], and because biochar moves below the plough layer or is lost by erosion [@major2010; @rumpel2006]. We represent this decline by $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ (@eq-bc-stock). The magnitude of the response was also fitted mainly to measurements in the first year after application (66% of field observations; Supplementary Text S3), so it may include transient effects of fresh biochar, such as the release of nutrients from its ash. Field trials are too short to estimate $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ precisely. In 70 series of repeated measurements from 23 studies, with a median follow-up of 1 year, it was 0.14 yr^-1^ (90% confidence interval −0.43 to 0.31), but its sign depends on a single study on acid soils [@cornelissen2013]. That decline is consistent with a fading liming effect, which the model values separately as avoided lime. On soils with a pH of 6.5 or above, where the response reflects CEC rather than liming, the response did not decline (Supplementary Text S3). Over longer periods, the yield benefit of a single application fades within 5–10 years in many long-term experiments, partly as its liming effect wanes [@yang2025biochar]. Yet charcoal-rich Anthrosols, such as the Terra Preta of Amazonia and the African Dark Earths, remain more fertile than adjacent soils centuries after the charcoal was added [@glaser2001; @liang2006; @solomon2016]. We therefore sample $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ from a PERT distribution with a minimum of zero, a mode of 0.05 yr^-1^ and a maximum of 0.3 yr^-1^ (@tbl-si-mc). The mode corresponds to a half-life of the response of about 14 years: slow enough to be consistent with the persistence on soils where the response reflects CEC and with the Anthrosols, and above zero to allow for occlusion, translocation and transient effects of fresh biochar. The maximum lies near the 95th percentile of the bootstrap estimates and covers the faster fading seen after single applications. The minimum of zero avoids extrapolating the short-term increases observed on some soils over decades.

### Residue minerals and ash return

The liming, P and K values of biochar and combustion ash follow from one mass and charge balance of the residue's mineral fraction (Ca, Mg, K, Na, P, Cl and S; see Spatial input data). The acid-neutralizing capacity of a residue is

$$Q = 2n_{\mathrm{Ca}} + 2n_{\mathrm{Mg}} + n_{\mathrm{K}} + n_{\mathrm{Na}} - n_{\mathrm{Cl}} - 2n_{\mathrm{S}} - n_{\mathrm{P}},$$ {#eq-anc}

where $n_i$ is the amount of element $i$ (mol Mg^-1^ of feedstock) and $Q$ (mol of charge Mg^-1^) is expressed as CaCO~3~ equivalent. Base cations balanced by weak-acid anions (carbonate, oxide, silicate and organic anions) neutralize soil acidity, whereas those balanced by chloride or sulfate do not. Phosphate counts as one equivalent because H~2~PO~4~^−^ is the dominant species at soil pH, and silica carries no alkalinity.

Biochar produced at about 500 °C retains all of the Ca, Mg, K, Na and P, 45% of the Cl and 40% of the S [@saleh2014; @knudsen2004]. In combustion, Cl and S leave the fuel bed as KCl and K~2~SO~4~, which make up most of the fly ash of straw-fired grate boilers [@thomsen2006]. We assign 90% of the Cl, 50% of the S and 5% of the P to the fly ash, together with the K bound by the Cl and S; the bottom ash retains the rest (Supplementary Text S2). Per megagram of feedstock, biochar therefore carries 13–16% more acid-neutralizing capacity than the bottom ash and 1.6–1.9 times its K.

All pathways are compared against the same counterfactual, in which the residue remains in the field or is combusted there (see Residue removal counterfactual). Each pathway is therefore charged for the nutrients and alkalinity that the counterfactual would have returned to the soil, and credited for those it returns in biochar or ash. The charge per megagram of feedstock is

$$C_{\mathrm{rem}} = (1 - f_{\mathrm{burn}})\, f_{\mathrm{N}}\, w_{\mathrm{N}}\, p_{\mathrm{N}} + w_{\mathrm{P}}\, p_{\mathrm{P}} + w_{\mathrm{K}}\, p_{\mathrm{K}} + \delta\, Q_{\mathrm{res}}\, p_{\mathrm{lime}},$$ {#eq-removal}

where $C_{\mathrm{rem}}$ is in US\$ Mg^-1^, $f_{\mathrm{burn}}$ is the share of the residue that would otherwise be combusted in the field (see Residue removal counterfactual), $w_{\mathrm{N}}$, $w_{\mathrm{P}}$ and $w_{\mathrm{K}}$ are the N, P and K contents of the residue (kg Mg^-1^; @tbl-parameters), $p_{\mathrm{N}}$, $p_{\mathrm{P}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{K}}$ their prices (US\$ kg^-1^), $f_{\mathrm{N}}$ the fertilizer replacement value of residue N (fraction), $Q_{\mathrm{res}}$ the acid-neutralizing capacity of the residue (@eq-anc, kg CaCO~3~-eq Mg^-1^), $p_{\mathrm{lime}}$ the lime cost (US\$ kg^-1^), and $\delta$ is 1 where soil pH is below the target pH and 0 elsewhere. Prices are those used for the nutrient and liming credits (see Biochar agronomic valuation), with N priced as urea. P, K and alkalinity are charged in full, because residues combusted in the field also return them in their ash. N is charged only on the share of residue that would have been retained, because it is lost when residues are combusted in the field. Its fertilizer replacement value, $f_{\mathrm{N}}$, is assumed to be zero. Cereal residues have a high C:N ratio, so their decomposition immobilizes mineral N in the soil, and subsequent crops recover little of their N: about 8% over three years in a ^15^N-labelled straw experiment [@thomsen1994]. That recovery is gross of the fertilizer N immobilized meanwhile, so it is an upper bound on the replacement value. The Monte Carlo analysis samples $f_{\mathrm{N}}$ up to 0.1 to cover it and the N-richer residues of soybean, which the cereal composition omits (@tbl-si-mc). The charge is the same for every pathway, so it does not change which technology is preferred, but it raises the cost of all of them.
