We do not include the emissions from manufacturing the fertilizer and lime that replace the nutrients and alkalinity removed, nor those avoided by the nutrients and alkalinity returned in biochar and ash. With residue N given no replacement value, these concern only P, K and lime. Biochar returns all of the P and K and more alkalinity than the residue. Bottom ash returns 95% of the P and 52–62% of the K, so for BE and BECCS the omitted emissions are those of producing the potash that replaces the K lost in fly ash, 4–9 kg K~2~O Mg^-1^ of feedstock.

Relative to the counterfactual, biochar returns all of the P and K and more alkalinity than the residue, because part of its Cl and S is volatilized in pyrolysis. The bottom ash from BE and BECCS is assumed to be returned to cropland, as at Danish straw-fired power plants. It is credited for its liming value where soil pH is below the target pH, and for its P and K at the same prices and on the same total-content basis as biochar. It is returned to the fields in the same way as biochar (see Biomass transport costs and emissions and Biochar field application), in one spreading pass at 5 Mg ha^-1^, the maximum allowed for straw ash in Denmark [@bioash2019]. Fly ash, which concentrates heavy metals, is assumed to be landfilled, so combustion loses the K, Cl and S that the fly ash holds. Because nearly all straw ash in Denmark is used as fertilizer or soil improver [@lamers2018], the share of fly ash returned to cropland is sampled from 0 to 1 in the Monte Carlo analysis. The cost of landfilling fly ash, below 1.5 US\$ Mg^-1^ of feedstock, is part of plant O&M.

## Baseline energy system and offsets

To robustly account for the climate mitigation benefit of bioenergy generation, the framework evaluates greenhouse gas offsets using a consequential Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) boundary. Total carbon abatement is calculated distinctively for each technology pathway, balancing active sequestration, grid displacement credits, and Scope 3 supply chain emissions.

### Net carbon abatement balances

The net carbon abatement for each grid cell is defined as the sum of physical carbon sequestered and emissions displaced, minus the transportation emissions penalty:

-   **BE:** Abatement relies entirely on the displacement of grid emissions, minus the Scope 3 emissions associated with diesel trucking of the biomass feedstock.
-   **BECCS:** Abatement includes the physical CO~2~ captured and injected into the geological sink (assuming a 90% capture rate) plus the grid displacement credit. However, because the parasitic energy load of the capture process reduces the net electrical efficiency, the total energy exported and thus the resulting grid displacement credit is proportionally lower for BECCS than for pure BE.
-   **PyCCS:** Abatement combines the grid displacement credit with the permanent CO~2~ equivalent of the biochar carbon retained in the soil ($S_{\mathrm{bc}}$; see Biochar carbon storage) and the avoided soil N~2~O emissions ($A_{\mathrm{N_2O}}$), minus the diesel emissions of biochar field application.

For BECCS, the emissions of CO~2~ transport are also deducted (see Maritime shipping and subsea pipelines). The residue removal counterfactual below applies to all pathways.

For all pathways, Scope 3 feedstock transport emissions are modeled dynamically by applying a heavy-duty diesel transport emissions factor ($0.0001\text{ Mg CO}_2\text{e}$ per $\text{Mg}\cdot\text{km}$, the well-to-wheel default for a 34–40 Mg articulated diesel truck at average load, including empty running [@glec2024]) to the effective biomass collection distance.

### Residue removal counterfactual

Removing crop residues for energy has two further effects on greenhouse gas balances that are common to all pathways, relative to a counterfactual in which residues remain in the field. First, retained residues add to soil organic carbon (SOC); residue retention increases SOC stocks by around 10% relative to removal [@bolinder2020]. Retained residues also add nitrogen to the soil and increase soil N~2~O emissions. Process-based simulations across more than 400 million hectares of cropland found that, through to 2100, the SOC gain and the N~2~O increase from retaining more residue approximately cancel almost everywhere, the Brazilian Cerrado being the main exception [@mcclelland2025]. The net soil GHG penalty of removal ($P_{soil}$, Mg CO~2~e per Mg feed) is therefore set to zero by default, and retained as a parameter for sensitivity analysis (@tbl-parameters). A penalty that counted the forgone SOC alone, without the offsetting N~2~O, would be about 0.19 Mg CO~2~e per Mg feed. Second, in regions where residues are commonly burned in the field, removal avoids the non-CO~2~ emissions from open burning (CO~2~ from burning is biogenic and is not counted). These are estimated with the IPCC Tier 1 emission factors for methane and nitrous oxide from burning agricultural residues and the associated combustion factor [@ipcc2006], applied to the share of the available residue in each grid cell that would otherwise be burned ($f_{burn}$). The burnt mass is estimated from the burnt share of cereal residue production in each 0.5° cell (2017–2021 mean) of a global cereal residue dataset that combines satellite fire observations with residue production [@smerald2023], multiplied by the cereal field residue production underlying the residue supply [@karan2023]; $f_{burn}$ is this mass divided by the available residue, both averaged to the model grid, and capped at 1. Using the burnt share rather than the burnt mass keeps the different residue totals of the two datasets out of the ratio. Burning of non-cereal residues, such as sugarcane trash, is not counted, and satellite fire products under-detect small field fires, so the estimate is conservative; a multiplier sampled from 0.5 to 1.5 represents this uncertainty in the Monte Carlo analysis. The biomass-weighted mean of $f_{burn}$ is 2% in the United States, 6% in Europe, 3% in China and 13% in India, and burning is concentrated in Punjab and Haryana in India, Ukraine and the Balkans in Europe, and north-eastern China:

$$A_{residue} = f_{burn} \cdot CF \cdot \left(EF_{CH_4} \cdot GWP_{CH_4} + EF_{N_2O} \cdot GWP_{N_2O}\right) \cdot 10^{-3} - P_{soil}$$

where $CF$ is the combustion factor, $EF$ the emission factors (g kg^-1^ dry matter), and $GWP$ the 100-year global warming potentials [@forster2021]; parameter values are given in @tbl-parameters. Because the same term applies to every pathway, it does not change which technology is preferred in a grid cell, but it changes the absolute net abatement and therefore shifts the marginal abatement cost curves.

### Grid displacement

The carbon intensity of the electricity displaced by bioenergy output depends on how far the energy system has decarbonized, which in turn depends on the carbon price. Because the carbon price $P$ is an exogenous input to the analysis, the displaced marginal emission factor (MEF) is modeled as a continuous function of $P$, so that the model does not combine a high carbon price with a fossil-dominated grid margin. Each grid cell's empirical build margin at today's explicit carbon price is used as an anchor and scaled by a regional price-response curve calibrated to integrated assessment scenarios.

**Empirical anchor.** New bioenergy capacity is assumed to displace the technology mix currently expanding on each grid. Using monthly national and US state electricity generation data [@ember2025], the sources with positive net generation growth ($\Delta G_i > 0$) between 2019 and 2024 are identified, and the build-margin intensity is their growth-weighted mean:

$$MEF_{emp} = \frac{\sum_i \Delta G_{i} \cdot CI_{i}}{\sum_i \Delta G_{i}}$$

where $CI_i$ is the IPCC median life-cycle greenhouse gas intensity of source $i$ [@schlomer2014]: coal (820 g CO~2~e kWh^-1^), natural gas (490), solar (48), geothermal (38), hydro (24), nuclear (12) and wind (11.5). Bioenergy generation is assigned zero intensity, because bioenergy emissions are accounted for explicitly in the model; growth in bioenergy generation still counts in the denominator. Where no growth data are available, the average grid intensity is used. The resulting anchors are 378 g CO~2~e kWh^-1^ for China and 574 for India, with medians over biomass-producing grid cells of 341 for the United States (state level) and 38 for Europe (country level).

**Price-response curve.** The decline of the displaced intensity with carbon price follows a Hill (log-logistic) curve,

$$MEF(P) = MEF_{min} + \left(MEF_{emp} - MEF_{min}\right) \frac{H(P)}{H(P_{now})}, \qquad H(P) = \frac{1}{1 + (P/P_{50})^{k}}$$

where $P_{now}$ is the region's current explicit carbon price on power-sector emissions (@tbl-parameters: the EU Emissions Trading System and China's national emissions trading scheme; no national price in the United States or India), so that the curve passes through each cell's empirical anchor at today's price. The scenario carbon price is thus interpreted as an explicit price: for a given explicit price, the curve gives the intensity of the electricity that new bioenergy capacity would displace, with today's non-price policies embedded in the empirical anchor. Prices below today's level imply a more carbon-intensive margin than observed, capped at the intensity of coal. $MEF_{min}$ = 20 g CO~2~e kWh^-1^ is the residual life-cycle intensity of a decarbonized grid [@pehl2017]. The midpoint price $P_{50}$ and steepness $k$ were fitted for each region to the NGFS Phase 5 scenarios (seven scenarios; GCAM 6.0 and MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM 2.0) [@ngfs2026], by robust least squares with equal model weights. GCAM reports the United States, India and the European Union as native regions. For MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM, whose native regions are larger aggregates, the NGFS country-level downscaled results for the United States, India and the EU-27 were used, with coal and gas generation divided into unabated and CCS shares according to the parent region. For each model, the fleet-average intensity of electricity generation at each five-year step was normalized by that model's own low-price value, so that only the shape of the decline, and not its level, is transferred to the empirical anchors. The fleet average was used rather than the models' build margin because, in these scenarios, new capacity is already predominantly renewable at zero carbon price, leaving the build margin with little price response; the fleet average tracks the decarbonization of the system that a baseload plant displaces over its lifetime. A two-stage variant (coal-to-gas switching, then decarbonization) was selected by the Akaike information criterion for Europe only; single-stage curves were imposed for China and India, where coal-to-gas switching is limited by gas availability. The fitted midpoints are $P_{50}$ = 103 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e for the United States, 53 for China and 44 for India, and 45 and 138 US\$ Mg^-1^ for the two stages in Europe (2024 USD). REMIND-MAgPIE was excluded from the fit because its grid decarbonizes over time even at low carbon prices, so that its price response could not be separated from its time trend. Parameter uncertainty is represented by 1,000 bootstrap draws over models and scenarios, which are sampled in the Monte Carlo analysis. Because the same carbon price values removals and emissions, the displaced intensity declines as the removal price rises.

## Regional cost adjustment

The combustion plant CAPEX of BE and BECCS is specified for each region directly (see Bioenergy (BE)). Other capital costs (pyrolysis plants, the PyCCS power block, pipelines, liquefaction and port terminals) are specified for a base location and scaled by a regional capital cost location factor, so that the relative cost of technologies is consistent within each region. O&M is charged at the same fraction of CAPEX in every region, so its absolute level follows regional CAPEX. The fraction does not fall where labour is cheaper: India's regulated O&M allowance for biomass plants is 7.8% of the regulated CAPEX per year [@cerc2024], compared with about 4% in the United States and Europe [@eia2026; @dea2020]. Biomass haulage costs are scaled by a regional road-freight cost factor (@tbl-parameters). <!-- TODO (reference required): CAPEX multipliers. -->

## Spatial input data

Crop residue availability is the sustainably harvestable residue of @karan2023 (net of residues retained for soil protection), minus the fraction fed to livestock [@herrero2013] (see Biomass feedstock sourcing and logistics). Feedstock composition is representative of cereal straws, corn stover and rice straw in the Phyllis2 database [@phyllis2]: 48% carbon and a lower heating value of 18.6 GJ Mg^-1^ on a dry, ash-free basis. The ash and mineral contents are the residue-weighted means of the cereal residue available in each region, using the median composition of each residue type in Phyllis2 (wheat, barley and other small-grain straws, maize stover and cob, rice straw and husk, sorghum and millet stalks; cereals are 74–85% of the harvestable residue in each region). Ash is 5.3% of dry mass in the United States, where maize stover predominates, 5.8% in Europe, 12.8% in China and 18.6% in India, where rice straw and husk make up 56% and 99% of the available cereal residue. Potassium contents are 8.0, 8.7, 12.7 and 16.3 kg Mg^-1^ of dry matter in the four regions (@tbl-parameters). Soil pH and cation exchange capacity (0–5 cm) are from SoilGrids 2.0 [@poggio2021] and mean annual soil temperature (0–5 cm) from the global soil bioclimatic maps of @lembrechts2022. Residue supply per hectare of harvested area (see Biochar field application) uses the MapSPAM 2010 harvested area of the crops in the residue data [@yu2020spam]. Cropping intensity, the ratio of harvested area to physical cropland excluding fallow land, is a regional value (@tbl-parameters); land-use assessments that ignore it overstate the cropland that crop production occupies [@waha2025]. Multiple cropping, mostly double cropping, covers about 36% of cropland in China, with triple cropping on a further 2–11% [@waha2020]. In India it covers 35–41% of cropland in national censuses; the gridded estimate of @waha2020 is lower, 16%, which its authors attribute to the crop calendars used for crops other than rice. We therefore use a cropping intensity of 1.4 for both China and India. Multiple cropping is rare in North America and Europe [@waha2020], where we assume a cropping intensity of 1. The value of crop production per hectare of harvested area, $v_{\mathrm{c}}$, is the MapSPAM 2010 production of the major field crops (cereals, roots and tubers, pulses, oilseeds, sugar crops and fibers) in each grid cell, valued at FAOSTAT producer prices [@faostat2025], divided by their harvested area. The price of each crop is the mean of national producer prices weighted by national production, averaged over 2019–2023 after escalation to 2024 USD. Electricity is valued at the wholesale price a generator receives, rather than at retail tariffs, whose regional differences largely reflect taxes, network charges and cross-subsidies. Prices are averages over 2024–2025, excluding the anomalous prices of the 2022 European gas crisis and its aftermath in 2023. For the United States, each state takes the price at the wholesale trading hub of the market that serves most of it (11 hubs) [@eia2026steo]. For Europe, prices are national day-ahead market prices [@ember2026price], with those of Türkiye [@epias2026] and Ukraine [@marketoperator2026] from their market operators; small markets without published prices take a neighbouring market's price. Belarus, which has no wholesale market, takes its industrial tariff [@climatescope2021] multiplied by the ratio of wholesale to industrial prices in the United States (median across states in 2024, 0.42) [@eia2026steo; @eia2025epa]. For China, the price is the provincial benchmark on-grid tariff for coal-fired power [@ndrc2019], which is also the reference price for renewable generators, excluding value-added tax. For India, it is the average price on the day-ahead market of the Indian Energy Exchange in 2024-25 [@cerc2025stm], a single national value because the market rarely separates into regional prices. Each year's price is converted at that year's average exchange rate [@worldbank2026fx] and escalated to 2024 US dollars. The biomass-weighted mean prices are 40 US\$ MWh^-1^ for the United States, 96 for Europe, 47 for China and 49 for India. Grid carbon intensities are described under Grid Displacement.

## Economic evaluation and technology selection

For each grid cell and technology, the net value per megagram of feedstock is the sum of revenues (electricity sales, the carbon price multiplied by the net abatement, and the agronomic value of biochar or ash) minus costs. The costs are annualized CAPEX, O&M, feedstock and haulage, the charge for the nutrients and alkalinity removed with the residue, the field application of biochar or ash, and, for BECCS, CO~2~ transport and storage. CAPEX is annualized with the capital recovery factor at the regional discount rate over the technology lifetime (25 years for BE and BECCS [@dea2026]; 20 years for the pyrolysis unit and 25 years for its power block [@woolf2016optimal]), so that all costs and revenues are levelized annual values per megagram of feedstock. Because O&M is a constant annual cost, discounting it over the plant lifetime and re-annualizing at the same rate returns the annual value. The agronomic effects of biochar and the cost of applying it accrue over the horizon $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ (see Biochar field application), which extends beyond the plant lifetime because biochar remains in the soil after the plant closes. They are discounted over this horizon and annualized over the plant lifetime:

$$V_x = \frac{\mathrm{CRF}(r, t_{\mathrm{L}})}{m} \sum_{t=1}^{t_{\mathrm{H}}} \frac{x_t}{(1+r)^t},$$ {#eq-ag-level}

where $V_x$ is the levelized value per megagram of feedstock (US\$ Mg^-1^), $x_t$ the benefit or cost per hectare of cropland in year $t$ (US\$ ha^-1^ yr^-1^), $m$ the feedstock supplied per hectare of cropland (Mg ha^-1^ yr^-1^), $\mathrm{CRF}(r, t_{\mathrm{L}})$ the capital recovery factor and $r$ the regional discount rate.

The regional discount rates (@tbl-parameters) are real, after-tax costs of capital for bioenergy projects: 5.6% for the United States, 6.8% for Europe, 6.2% for China and 7.1% for India. They are the nominal costs of capital in US dollars projected for 2030 by @hatton2025, converted to real terms with an expected inflation rate of 2.5%. We use after-tax rates, as is usual in techno-economic assessment. Grossing them up to pre-tax rates at statutory corporate tax rates [@enache2024] would add 3–4 percentage points, but would overstate the effective tax burden, which depreciation allowances reduce. Real rates are required because all cash flows, including the carbon price, are expressed in constant 2024 US dollars. All costs are in 2024 US dollars: values from other years are escalated with the US consumer price index (CPI-U), and values in other currencies are converted at the average exchange rate of the source year before escalation. The plant has a thermal input of 125 MW~th~ by default, and the preferred technology in each cell is the one with the highest net value. Because the displaced grid intensity falls as the carbon price rises (see Grid displacement), net abatement, and hence net value, is not linear in the carbon price. We therefore evaluate the model on a grid of carbon prices (0–250 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e in steps of 5 US\$ Mg^-1^, and 275–500 US\$ Mg^-1^ in steps of 25 US\$ Mg^-1^) and interpolate abatement linearly between grid points; net value is the carbon-price-independent part plus the carbon price multiplied by the interpolated abatement (for PyCCS, both parts are those of the energy configuration and application strategy chosen at each price). The break-even carbon price of a technology is the lowest carbon price at which its net value becomes non-negative. Marginal abatement cost curves assign each grid cell, at each carbon price, to the technology with the highest net value if that value is non-negative, and sum the biomass, area and abatement of the assigned cells.

## Statistical methods

Parameter uncertainty was propagated by Monte Carlo simulation, with 5,000 draws per region. Each parameter with an uncertainty range was sampled from a PERT or uniform distribution, with the central values, distributions and bounds listed in @tbl-si-mc, and correlated parameters were sampled jointly through a Gaussian copula. The uncertainty of the grid displacement curve was represented by sampling one of its 1,000 bootstrap draws in each iteration. The drivers of each technology's net value were identified by fitting gradient-boosted regression trees [XGBoost; @chen2016xgboost] to the Monte Carlo results and computing SHAP values [@lundberg2017]. The same method was applied across grid cells, to the choice of preferred technology, to identify its spatial drivers. Structural assumptions that the Monte Carlo analysis holds fixed were tested with the same carbon-price sweep as the marginal abatement cost curves, at the regional discount rates: plant sizes of 50 and 250 MW~th~ either side of the default of 125 MW~th~, dedicated pipelines instead of shared trunklines (each plant builds its own pipeline over the full distance to the sink), and CO~2~-EOR allowed as a sink (@fig-si-variants). Plant size is treated as a design assumption rather than optimised. When the model chooses the size that maximises net value in each cell, it tends towards the largest size considered, because economies of scale outweigh the longer haulage, implying gigawatt-scale plants throughout agricultural landscapes. In practice, plant size is limited by constraints outside the model, such as the road traffic and nuisance of continuous truck deliveries and the capacity of local roads and grid connections, so the default of 125 MW~th~ is large compared with typical biomass plants but not exceptional, and the size variants show the sensitivity of the results to this assumption.

To identify which spatial inputs determine the optimal technology in each grid cell, we fitted a surrogate classifier to the spatial sensitivity results (scenario CP100_MW250: carbon price 100 US\$ Mg^-1^ CO~2~e, plant size 250 MW~th~) and attributed its predictions to the inputs with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values [@chen2016xgboost]. The classifier is a gradient-boosted tree ensemble (XGBoost; multi-class soft-probability objective, maximum depth 6, learning rate 0.05, 120 rounds) that predicts the technology with the highest net value (BE, BECCS or PyCCS) from ten cell-level inputs: biomass density, soil temperature, electricity price, field-side feedstock cost, the length of the CO~2~ route chosen by BECCS, whether that route ends at an offshore sink, the storage cost at that sink, soil pH, soil cation exchange capacity (CEC) and the displaced grid carbon intensity. SHAP values are in log-odds of each class.

Two kinds of model are fitted. A global model, fitted to all four regions together, shows which inputs distinguish the regions as well as cells within them. Because some inputs are constant within a region (for example, feedstock cost outside Europe and the electricity price in India), in the global model they partly act as labels for the region rather than as drivers of within-region variation. A separate model is therefore fitted for each region; inputs that are constant within the region are dropped. The regional models are used for the maps of the dominant driver (@fig-shap-dominant, @fig-shap-magnitude) and for the regional beeswarm and dependence plots (@fig-si-bee-global to @fig-si-bee-india and the dependence plots that follow them); @tbl-si-shap-importance gives the share of each input in the mean absolute SHAP value of each model. Beeswarm and dependence plots show a random sample of 20,000 cells per model; SHAP values were computed for all cells. In the dependence plots, points are coloured by the input with the strongest estimated interaction with the plotted input.

## Model parameters and data sources

Parameters utilized within the C-SCAPE model are shown in @tbl-parameters, classified by their spatial resolution: "scalar" parameters are constant globally; "regional" parameters take region-specific values; and "spatial" values are resolved at the grid-cell level.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-parameters
#| tbl-cap: "Operational, financial, and biophysical parameters of the C-SCAPE model."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(gt)
library(dplyr)

raw_params <- read.csv("../BiocharAG/inst/extdata/parameters.csv", check.names = FALSE, na.strings = "")

# Units in parameters.csv use Pandoc markdown (Mg^-1^, CO~2~); tables need LaTeX (or HTML) markup
md_units <- function(x, latex = knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- ""
  if (latex) {
    x <- gsub("([$%&_#])", "\\\\\\1", x)
    x <- gsub("\\^([^^]+)\\^", "\\\\textsuperscript{\\1}", x)
    gsub("~([^~]+)~", "\\\\textsubscript{\\1}", x)
  } else {
    x <- gsub("\\^([^^]+)\\^", "<sup>\\1</sup>", x)
    gsub("~([^~]+)~", "<sub>\\1</sub>", x)
  }
}

# Filter out rows that shouldn't be displayed
# Exclude Constants, Control Flags, and some spatial metrics
display_df <- raw_params |>
  filter(!(category %in% c("Constants", "Control Flags"))) |>
  filter(!(name %in% c("avg_dist", "collection_radius", "dist_offshore", "dist_onshore", "dist_sink_km", "dist_sink_saline_km", "feedstock_cost", "plant_sizes_mw_th", "flat_ci_tCO2_GJ", "rebound",
    # BEBCS heat mode: optional, not used in the results (see Discussion)
    "bebcs_heat_capital_cost", "bebcs_heat_efficiency", "bebcs_heat_life", "bebcs_heat_om_factor",
    "heat_price", "heat_boiler_ci", "heat_pump_cop", "heat_offtake"))) |>
  select(
    Category = category,
    Parameter = name,
    Description = description,
    USA = US,
    Europe = Europe,
    China = China,
    India = India,
    Units = units
  ) |>
  mutate(Units = md_units(Units)) |>
  mutate(
    # Convert NA to Spatially explicit for regional columns
    USA = ifelse(is.na(USA), "Spatially explicit", USA),
    Europe = ifelse(is.na(Europe), "Spatially explicit", Europe),
    China = ifelse(is.na(China), "Spatially explicit", China),
    India = ifelse(is.na(India), "Spatially explicit", India),
    # Add backticks to Parameter names for markdown formatting
    Parameter = paste0("`", Parameter, "`")
  ) |>
  # Arrange by Category
  arrange(Category)

# Identify rows where all regional values are identical
is_uniform <- with(display_df, !is.na(USA) & USA == Europe & Europe == China & China == India & USA != "Spatially explicit")

display_df$Europe[is_uniform] <- ""
display_df$China[is_uniform] <- ""
display_df$India[is_uniform] <- ""

gt(display_df, groupname_col = "Category") |>
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Value",
    columns = c(USA, Europe, China, India)
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Parameter = "Parameter",
    Description = "Description",
    USA = "USA/Default",
    Europe = "Europe",
    China = "China",
    India = "India",
    Units = "Units"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    Parameter ~ pct(18),
    Description ~ pct(24),
    USA ~ pct(12),
    Europe ~ pct(10),
    China ~ pct(10),
    India ~ pct(10),
    Units ~ pct(16)
  ) |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = c(Category, Parameter, Description, USA, Europe, China, India)) |>
  fmt_passthrough(columns = Units, escape = FALSE) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(9),
    data_row.padding = px(2),
    row_group.font.weight = "bold",
    latex.use_longtable = TRUE,
    latex.header_repeat = TRUE
  )
```

## Supplementary Text {.unnumbered}

### Text S1. Capacity factors and price capture of biomass power {.unnumbered}

Technology data give an availability of 91% for biomass plants [@dea2026], but this accounts only for planned and unplanned outages, not for operation below full output, which depends on how each technology is dispatched. Historical capacity factors of biomass power plants, such as 0.54–0.61 for US wood-fired plants over the past decade [@eia2026epm] and 0.50–0.64 for Drax's biomass units in 2023–2024 [@drax2025], reflect dispatch in grids with low or no carbon prices and are a poor guide to operation in decarbonizing grids. Models that optimize capacity and hourly dispatch together under carbon constraints find two roles for biomass power. Firm, base-load low-carbon supply [@daggash2019; @prado2023] is favored at high CO~2~ charges where other sources of flexibility are ample [@ahlstrom2022]. Flexible supply serves hours of high residual load in systems dominated by wind and solar [@johansson2019; @lehtveer2021]. We therefore evaluate BE in both modes: base load at a capacity factor of 0.85 (Monte Carlo range 0.75–0.90) and flexible operation at 0.45 (range 0.30–0.60).

A plant that follows prices sells in high-price hours, so its realized price exceeds the time-averaged wholesale price. We estimated this ratio from hourly day-ahead prices in 24–31 European markets over 2015–2025 [@ember2026hourly], for a plant that runs the highest-priced hours of each day among its available hours (availability 0.91), with perfect foresight and no start-up or minimum-load constraints. The median ratio across markets in 2024–2025 was 1.05 at a capacity factor of 0.85 and 1.30 at 0.45 (10th–90th percentile 1.19–1.42); the latter has risen from 1.15–1.21 in 2015–2023 as solar generation has grown. Grid storage bounds the daily price spread available to a flexible generator: prices in discharge hours cannot persistently exceed the charging price divided by the round-trip efficiency plus the levelized cost of storage. At 65 US\$ MWh^-1^ for utility-scale batteries [@ember2025battery], this gives about 1.34 times the average European price, and about 1.9 at the US costs of @lazard2025. Batteries do not shift energy between seasons or across multi-day lulls in wind, whereas stored biomass can, and models of decarbonized systems show a wider spread of prices, with more hours at both very low and high prices [@geis2025]. The ratios are therefore 1.05 (range 1.02–1.08) for base load and 1.30 (range 1.15–1.45) for flexible operation, applied in all regions; they are derived from European markets and are an assumption elsewhere. The allocation between modes also depends on the generation mix and demand of each grid, which are not modeled.

BECCS is driven towards base-load operation by its higher capital cost, by removal revenue earned per megagram of CO~2~ captured, and by the need to keep the capture plant, dense-phase pipeline and injection in steady operation [@johansson2019; @prado2023]. It takes 0.85, the design capacity factor of CCS power plants [@petranova2020], with a range of 0.60–0.90; the lower end reflects operation of about 3,900 full-load hours where scarce biomass is directed to high-price hours [@lehtveer2021]. Electricity is a small share of PyCCS revenue, so its operation is limited by the availability of the pyrolysis unit and the continuity of biomass supply rather than by dispatch. It takes 0.80 (range 0.70–0.85), below the 0.90 on-stream factor of nth-plant pyrolysis designs [@dutta2015], to allow for interruptions of feedstock supply.

### Text S2. Partition of residue minerals in combustion and pyrolysis {.unnumbered}

Biochar produced at about 500 °C retains all of the Ca, Mg, K, Na and P of the feedstock, and 45% of the Cl and 40% of the S. The remainder is released as HCl and sulfur gases, which raises the acid-neutralizing capacity of the char [@saleh2014; @knudsen2004]. In combustion, Cl and S leave the fuel bed as KCl and K~2~SO~4~, which make up most of the fly ash of straw-fired grate boilers (53% KCl and 29% K~2~SO~4~ at Avedøre [@thomsen2006]). We assign 90% of the Cl and 50% of the S to the fly ash, together with the K they bind and 5% of the P. The fly ash therefore has negligible acid-neutralizing capacity and holds 38–48% of the feedstock K; the bottom ash retains the Ca, Mg and Na and the remaining K and P. These assumptions give fly ash 15–18% of the ash mass for wheat and maize residues and 8–9% for rice residues, consistent with the 80–90% share of bottom ash reported for grate firing of straw [@lamers2018].

### Text S3. Meta-analysis of biochar field trials {.unnumbered}

We combined three compilations of field and pot trials that report crop yields with and without biochar: the data underlying the yield model of @woolf2016optimal, @xu2021 and @zhang2023. @xu2021 also report N~2~O emissions. The effect size is the natural logarithm of the ratio of the treatment and control means (log response ratio, lnRR), with its sampling variance calculated from the reported standard deviations and replicate numbers where available.

Three corrections were made before analysis. First, in @xu2021, treatments that combine biochar with another input, such as N fertilizer or manure, are compared with the same control as biochar alone in 27 of the 33 studies that report both. These contrasts include the effect of the input itself: their mean lnRR was 0.24–0.38, against 0.15 for biochar alone. We retained such a contrast only where its control differed from that of biochar alone, and otherwise calculated it against the treatment with the input alone (94 contrasts). For the same reason, three studies in @zhang2023 whose control yield did not vary with the N rate were excluded. The data of @woolf2016optimal use controls with the same fertilization as the biochar treatment. <!-- TODO: confirm --> Second, 15 studies appear in more than one compilation. They were matched on first author, year, dose and site, and retained once. Third, four studies that @woolf2016optimal coded as pot trials, and one column experiment, are labeled as field trials in @xu2021; we recoded them. Pot trials were excluded from all analyses, because their response to dose differs from that of field trials.

The shape of the yield response to dose was estimated within experiments, defined as sets of treatments that differ only in biochar dose (same study, site, crop, year, fertilization and biochar). For experiment $e$ and dose $D$, $\mathrm{lnRR}_{e,D} = \alpha_e (D/B_{\mathrm{r}})^{\gamma}$, with a separate magnitude $\alpha_e$ for each experiment. Differences between sites therefore do not affect $\gamma$, which is identified only by dose contrasts within experiments. The model was fitted by weighted least squares, with weights equal to the inverse of the sampling variance plus the residual variance between observations. Confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling of studies. Across 251 field experiments from 115 studies, $\gamma$ was 0.50 (90% confidence interval 0.29–0.66). It was 0.30 (0.16–0.46) on soils with a pH of 6.5 or above (100 experiments, 50 studies) and 0.64 (0.38–0.77) on soils below pH 6.0 (99 experiments, 41 studies), where the response includes a liming effect that is close to linear in dose. A saturating exponential fitted the data less well than the power function, and the response relative to that at 10–20 Mg ha^-1^ continued to increase above 40 Mg ha^-1^ (@fig-si-dose-response, panel a).

The magnitude of the response was modeled from all 1,264 field observations (191 studies). Each observation was normalized to the reference stock with the exponent of its soil pH class (0.30 at pH ≥ 6.5, 0.64 below 6.0, 0.50 between), giving $\alpha_i = \mathrm{lnRR}_i\, (B_{\mathrm{r}}/D_i)^{\gamma}$. We fitted multilevel meta-regressions with a random effect for each study and compared them with boosted regression trees and random forests by tenfold cross-validation in which whole studies were held out. The models predicted between-study variation only modestly. On the 51 studies that report both soil pH and CEC (434 observations), the share of the variance in study means explained by held-out predictions was 0.20 for a meta-regression on pH and CEC, 0.25 for boosted trees on pH and CEC, and 0.32 for a random forest on all covariates. Cross-validation that ignored the grouping of observations by study gave 0.38, which overstates predictive skill. Because the differences between methods are small relative to their uncertainty and global maps of pH and CEC are available, we used the meta-regression:

$$\alpha = \beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{A}} \max(0,\, 6.5 - \mathrm{pH}) + \beta_{\mathrm{C}} \ln \mathrm{CEC},$$

with $\beta_0$ = 0.361 (standard error 0.076), $\beta_{\mathrm{A}}$ = 0.070 (0.029) and $\beta_{\mathrm{C}}$ = −0.101 (0.025). Across the 10th to 90th percentiles of the observations, the pH term changes $\alpha$ by 0.15 and the CEC term by 0.24, consistent with the comparable importance of pH and CEC in @woolf2016optimal. In soils with pH of 6.5 or above alone (19 studies), $\beta_{\mathrm{C}}$ was −0.049 (0.042), so the CEC effect is identified mainly in acid soils, where low CEC and low pH occur together. C-SCAPE uses $\beta_0$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{C}}$ (@eq-yield-response), which the Monte Carlo analysis samples from a bivariate normal distribution with their estimated means and covariance. The weaker response fitted to soils with a pH of 6.5 or above alone ($\beta_0$ = 0.213, $\beta_{\mathrm{C}}$ = −0.049) lies outside the 90% range of these draws and is not sampled.

For N~2~O, 99 contrasts of biochar combined with another input were excluded because their controls lacked that input, and 7 duplicated rows were removed. The remaining 160 observations from 36 studies gave a mean lnRR of −0.224 (standard error 0.068) in a multilevel random-effects model with study and observation random effects, a reduction of 20% (90% confidence interval 11–29%). The log-dose slope was 0.001 (0.052) across studies, and dose contrasts within 44 experiments from 20 studies showed no trend (median difference 0.00). The reduction did not differ significantly between trials of less than and more than one year, but only 25 observations from 6 studies exceed one year.

Persistence of the yield response was examined in 70 series of the same treatment observed in two or more years (23 studies; median follow-up 1 year, maximum 5 years; 9 studies followed for 2 years or more). We fitted $\mathrm{lnRR}_{s,t} = \alpha_s e^{-k_{\mathrm{y}} t}$, with a separate magnitude $\alpha_s$ for each series and $t$ the time since the first observation. The estimated $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ was 0.14 yr^-1^ (90% confidence interval −0.43 to 0.31, by bootstrap resampling of studies), and its sign depends on a single study. Without the trials of @cornelissen2013, on acid soils, $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ was −0.30 yr^-1^. On soils with a pH of 6.5 or above (37 series, 11 studies), the response did not decline ($k_{\mathrm{y}}$ = −0.36 yr^-1^; 80% confidence interval −0.57 to 0.03), and omitting any one study left the estimate between −0.44 and −0.18 yr^-1^. The decline in the pooled data is thus concentrated in acid soils, where part of the response is a liming effect that diminishes as the soil reacidifies. Among series with an initial response above 0.05, the median response relative to the first observation was 0.83 after about one year (29 series, 15 studies) and 0.62 after about two years (10 series, 6 studies). These ratios overstate decline, because selecting series on a large first response favors subsequent regression toward the mean. Here $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ is the decline rate of the response itself; the model converts it to a decay of the effective biochar stock (@eq-bc-stock). The Monte Carlo distribution of $k_{\mathrm{y}}$ has its upper bound near the 95th percentile of the bootstrap estimates. Its mode of 0.05 yr^-1^, a half-life of about 14 years, gives more weight than the pooled estimate does to soils where the response reflects CEC rather than liming, while allowing for slow decline from occlusion, translocation and transient effects of fresh biochar (see Biochar agronomic valuation). Its lower bound of zero excludes extrapolating the short-term increases observed on some soils to decades. <!-- TODO: name the software used for the meta-analysis, with citation -->

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: tbl-si-mc
#| tbl-cap: "Parameters sampled in the Monte Carlo analysis, including central values (by region where they differ), distribution and range. Ranges marked “× central” are multipliers of the central value; other ranges are in the parameter's units. Where a bound differs by region it is shown in parentheses. For spatially explicit inputs, the relative range is applied as a multiplier on the spatial layer."
#| 
library(dplyr)
library(kableExtra)

raw <- read.csv("../BiocharAG/inst/extdata/parameters.csv", check.names = FALSE, na.strings = "")
regions <- c("US", "Europe", "China", "India")
fmt_num <- function(x) {
  v <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  ifelse(is.na(v), as.character(x), format(signif(v, 4), scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE, trim = TRUE))
}
fmt_num1 <- function(x) vapply(x, fmt_num, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
# Split a bound such as "0.85;India=0.5" into its base value and regional overrides
parse_bound <- function(b) {
  parts <- strsplit(as.character(b), ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  ov <- if (length(parts) > 1) {
    kv <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(parts[-1], "=", fixed = TRUE))
    stats::setNames(kv[, 2], kv[, 1])
  } else character(0)
  list(base = parts[1], ov = ov)
}
fmt_range <- function(lo, hi, rel) {
  a <- parse_bound(lo); b <- parse_bound(hi)
  unit <- if (rel) " × central" else ""
  out <- paste0(fmt_num(a$base), "–", fmt_num(b$base), unit)
  ovr <- union(names(a$ov), names(b$ov))
  if (length(ovr)) {
    extra <- vapply(ovr, function(r) {
      l <- if (r %in% names(a$ov)) a$ov[[r]] else a$base
      h <- if (r %in% names(b$ov)) b$ov[[r]] else b$base
      paste0(r, " ", fmt_num(l), "–", fmt_num(h))
    }, character(1))
    out <- paste0(out, " (", paste(extra, collapse = "; "), ")")
  }
  out
}
central <- function(row) {
  v <- unlist(row[regions])
  if (all(is.na(v))) return(paste0(fmt_num(row[["default_value"]]), " (spatial)"))
  if (length(unique(v)) == 1) return(fmt_num(v[1]))
  paste(paste(regions, fmt_num1(v)), collapse = "; ")
}

mc <- raw |> filter(!is.na(distribution), distribution != "none") |> arrange(category, name)
esc <- if (knitr::is_latex_output()) function(x) gsub("([$%&_#])", "\\\\\\1", x) else identity # escape = FALSE below
tab <- data.frame(
  Parameter = esc(mc$name),
  Description = esc(mc$description),
  Units = md_units(mc$units),
  Central = vapply(seq_len(nrow(mc)), function(i) central(mc[i, ]), character(1)),
  Dist. = tools::toTitleCase(mc$distribution),
  Range = vapply(seq_len(nrow(mc)), function(i) fmt_range(mc$dist_min[i], mc$dist_max[i], mc$dist_bounds[i] == "relative"), character(1))
)
grp <- rle(mc$category)
k <- kbl(tab, format = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "html", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"), font_size = 7) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3.3cm", monospace = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(2, width = "4.1cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2.1cm") |>
  column_spec(4, width = "2.2cm") |>
  column_spec(5, width = "0.9cm") |>
  column_spec(6, width = "2.6cm")
start <- 1
for (g in seq_along(grp$lengths)) {
  grp_label <- md_units(grp$values[g])
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) grp_label <- gsub("\\\\&", "\\\\\\\\&", grp_label)
  k <- pack_rows(k, grp_label, start, start + grp$lengths[g] - 1, escape = FALSE)
  start <- start + grp$lengths[g]
}
k
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: tbl-si-shap-importance
#| tbl-cap: "Share of mean absolute SHAP value (%, summed over classes) by input and model, and the training accuracy of each classifier. A dash marks an input that is constant within the region and was dropped from that region's model."
imp <- read.csv("results/spatial_shap/shap_importance_by_model.csv")
labs <- c(biomass_density = "Biomass density", soil_temp = "Soil temperature", elec_price = "Electricity price",
  feedstock_cost = "Feedstock cost", co2_route_km = "CO~2~ route length", co2_offshore = "Offshore CO~2~ sink",
  co2_storage_cost = "CO~2~ storage cost", soil_ph = "Soil pH", soil_cec = "Soil CEC",
  ff_c_intensity = "Grid carbon intensity")
models <- intersect(c("Global", "US", "Europe", "China", "India"), unique(imp$model))
tab <- data.frame(Input = unname(labs))
for (m in models) {
  s <- imp[imp$model == m, ]
  tab[[m]] <- ifelse(names(labs) %in% s$feature, sprintf("%.1f", s$share_pct[match(names(labs), s$feature)]), "–")
}
g <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(tab$Global))
tab <- tab[order(-ifelse(is.na(g), -1, g)), ] # by global importance
acc <- vapply(models, function(m) sprintf("%.1f", imp$accuracy_pct[imp$model == m][1]), character(1))
tab <- rbind(tab, c("Training accuracy", acc))
knitr::kable(tab, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("r", length(models)))) # pipe: Pandoc renders CO~2~
```

```{r}
for (f in dep) {

    parts[2], nm[parts[1]], f, lab))
}
```
